The Court of Master Sommeliers (CMS) has invalidated the results of the 2018 Master Sommelier Diploma Examination due to a breach of confidentiality, affecting 23 of the 24 newly minted master sommeliers. This decision, made by the CMS board chairman Devon Broglie, MS, was based on evidence that a master sommelier disclosed information about the tasting portion of the exam before it took place. The affected sommeliers, including Andrey Ivanov, Scott Barber, Vincent Morrow, and Robert Ord, will have two opportunities to retake the tasting exam, with the first chance in late 2018 and the second in 2019. All testing fees will be refunded, and travel expenses will be covered.

The CMS emphasized the importance of maintaining the integrity of the examination process, stating that a compromised exam would undermine the value of the Master Sommelier title. The board has barred the offending master sommelier from participating in any CMS programs and is initiating the process to terminate his membership. The decision has sent shockwaves through the sommelier community, which values the rigorous and prestigious exams administered by the CMS.

The sommelier community, which is already small and tightly knit, is now grappling with the implications of this scandal. The CMS's commitment to maintaining the integrity of the examination process underscores the high stakes involved in passing the master sommelier exam.

A study published in JAMA Internal Medicine found that individuals who felt younger than their actual age had a lower death rate compared to those who felt their age or older. The research, conducted by Isla Rippon and Dr. Andrew Steptoe from University College London, analyzed data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, involving 6,489 participants over an 8.25-year follow-up period. The average chronological age was 65.8 years, while the average self-perceived age was 56.8 years. Participants were categorized into three groups: those whose self-perceived age was close to their actual age, those who felt more than 1 year older, and those who felt 3 or more years younger.

The mortality rate was 14.3% among those who felt younger than their actual age, 18.0% for those with a self-perceived age close to their actual age, and 24.6% for those who felt older. The study also found a strong association between self-perceived age and death caused by cardiovascular disease, but not with cancer deaths. After adjusting for baseline health, physical disability, and health behaviors, the mortality hazard was 41% greater in those who felt older than their actual age.

The authors suggest that resilience, a sense of empowerment, and positive health behaviors might explain the lower mortality rates in those who felt younger. They conclude that self-perceived age has the potential to change and could be targeted with health messages promoting positive attitudes toward aging. The study highlights the importance of psychological well-being in aging and suggests that interventions aimed at improving self-perception could potentially reduce mortality rates.

This research adds to the growing body of evidence that psychological factors play a significant role in health outcomes, particularly in older adults. It underscores the importance of addressing mental health and well-being in aging populations to improve overall health and longevity.

Max Spiers, a British conspiracy theorist and UFO researcher, was found dead in Warsaw, Poland, on July 16, 2018. His mother, Vanessa Bates, believes his death was suspicious due to his recent investigations into UFOs and alleged government cover-ups. Polish authorities stated that Spiers died from natural causes, but no post-mortem was conducted, and his mother claims she was denied access to his paperwork. Spiers had a history of researching UFOs and claimed to have seen children in an underground alien base in New Mexico. His theories, while considered far-fetched by many, have gained a following among conspiracy theorists.

Scott C. Waring of UFO Sightings Daily suggested that Spiers' death might be part of a broader campaign to suppress UFO research. However, Nick Pope, who investigated UFO phenomena for the UK Ministry of Defence, denied any such clandestine operations. The Foreign Office stated that it would not investigate Spiers' death as it occurred abroad, and the Polish authorities are handling the investigation.

Bates has expressed her concerns, stating that Spiers was "incredibly strong" and unlikely to have died of natural causes. She believes he may have been targeted due to his investigations. Spiers had a history of health issues, including migraines and vomiting, in the days leading up to his death. His burial in Canterbury, England, allowed for a post-mortem examination, but the results are still pending.

The case has sparked speculation and debate among conspiracy theorists and UFO researchers, with some believing that Spiers' death might have been a result of his investigations. His theories, including the belief that Zionists and Nazis are working together and the existence of an alien base in New Mexico, have fueled the speculation.

Archaeologists have discovered 39 ingots of orichalcum, a mysterious and valuable metal from ancient Greek texts, off the coast of Gela, Sicily. These ingots, dating back to the 680s BCE, were likely part of a shipwreck that occurred around 2,600 years ago. The ingots, composed of 75-80% copper, 15-20% zinc, and small amounts of other metals, were probably transported from Greece or Asia Minor to Gela. The find, confirmed by X-ray fluorescence analysis, represents the first physical evidence of orichalcum, a metal previously known only through ancient texts and a few ornamental objects.

The discovery highlights Gela's wealth and artisanal capabilities in the 6th century BCE, as the city had only been founded about 100 years prior. The orichalcum ingots were likely destined for local workshops, where they would be used in high-quality decorations. The metal, described by Plato as second only to gold, was believed to have been mined in Atlantis and used to cover the walls of Poseidon's temple.

While most scholars agree that orichalcum was a brass-like alloy, some, like Enrico Mattievich, argue that it may have originated from the Peruvian Andes and was made of a different alloy. Mattievich suggests that the ancient Greeks may have discovered America, where a similar metallic alloy was found in Chavín civilization artifacts.

The Soprintendenza del Mare plans to excavate the shipwreck to uncover the full cargo, which could provide valuable insights into Sicily's ancient economic history. This discovery underscores the importance of continuing underwater archaeology to uncover hidden treasures and refine our understanding of ancient civilizations.

On August 14, 2013, a UPS cargo jet crashed shortly before reaching the runway at Birmingham-Shuttlesworth International Airport in Alabama. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) and FBI conducted an investigation, revealing that the flight recorder captured two audible warnings in the cockpit 16 seconds before impact, indicating the aircraft was descending at an abnormal rate for its altitude. However, the cause of the crash remains undetermined. The aircraft, a twin-engine Airbus A300, was attempting to land on the shorter Runway 18, which is 5,000 feet shorter than the main runway and lacks full instrument landing systems, making it challenging for pilots to judge altitude accurately. The captain, Cerea Beal, Jr., and first officer, Shanda Fanning, were both experienced pilots, but it is unclear if either had previously landed on Runway 18. The NTSB will analyze the aircraft's weight and assess the runway's lighting and navigation systems. The crash site is near a large hill and trees, and the plane hit a tree before crashing into the hill. The NTSB will investigate why the aircraft was too low to avoid the trees, and whether the shorter runway was the best option given the closure of the main runway. Witness accounts and the flight's descent pattern suggest the plane may have been using a "dive and drive" method typical for such runways.

The leaked transcripts of President Donald Trump's January 2017 phone calls with Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull reveal a deeply flawed and often incoherent leader. Trump's conversations with both leaders were marked by his inability to grasp the nuances of their policies and his focus on his own image and political interests.

In the call with Peña Nieto, Trump aggressively pushed for Mexico to pay for the border wall, even going so far as to call New Hampshire a "drug-infested den" to justify his stance. He also expressed a desire to impose tariffs on Mexico, despite not having discussed this with Mexican officials. Trump's comments were often dismissive and confrontational, reflecting his tendency to prioritize his own narrative over factual information.

The conversation with Turnbull was even more contentious. Trump was upset about an agreement made by the Obama administration to accept 1,250 refugees from Australia, whom Turnbull explained were economic refugees and had been vetted by both countries. Trump repeatedly dismissed Turnbull's explanations, calling the refugees "prisoners" and expressing concern that they might become terrorists. He also inflated the number of refugees to 2,000 and 5,000, showing a lack of understanding of the actual numbers involved.

Trump's inability to comprehend the policies and their rationale is evident throughout the transcripts. He failed to grasp that the Australian policy of detaining refugees who arrive by boat is a deterrent to illegal migration, not a reflection of their dangerousness. His comments reveal a profound misunderstanding of the complexities of international relations and refugee policies.

The transcripts also highlight Trump's narcissistic tendencies and his desire to maintain a positive public image, even at the expense of diplomatic relations. He frequently boasted about his campaign successes and his ability to connect with voters, often in a self-aggrandizing manner.

The leak of these transcripts suggests that there are internal conflicts within the White House, with some officials seeking to undermine Trump's erratic leadership. The nature of the leak, which portrays Trump in a negative light but does not compromise national security, indicates that it may have come from someone within the administration who is concerned about the national security implications of Trump's behavior.

Overall, the transcripts paint a picture of a president who is mentally limited and prone to making impulsive and poorly informed decisions, potentially damaging both domestic and international relations. The leak serves as a stark reminder of the challenges facing the administration and the need for better norms and discipline within the White House.

Moe’s Southwest Grill has recently overtaken Chipotle Mexican Grill to become the most favored Mexican-inspired fast-casual restaurant in the United States, according to the latest Harris Poll. This marks a significant shift, as Chipotle had held the top spot for the past three consecutive years. The Denver-based Chipotle chain has faced numerous food safety issues, including norovirus, salmonella, and E. coli outbreaks, which have led to a 30% decline in sales and a 33% drop in share prices. These challenges have also affected the brand's reputation, with customers increasingly turning to alternatives like Taco Bell, Qdoba Mexican Grill, and Baja Fresh Mexican Grill.

Moe’s, with its 600-unit chain, has seen a significant increase in brand equity, marking its first-ever top finish in the Harris Poll. The company has been praised for its responsiveness to customer feedback and its willingness to innovate, such as offering build-your-own taco and burrito bowls. Moe’s has also capitalized on Chipotle’s struggles, experiencing a 5% increase in foot traffic, as indicated by a Placed survey. Despite these gains, Moe’s still lags behind Chipotle in terms of market share and sales, with only 2.3% of the U.S. population visiting a Moe’s compared to nearly 9.4% visiting a Chipotle.

Chipotle’s decline can be attributed to a combination of factors, including the aforementioned food safety issues and a lack of new menu innovations. The company has attempted to regain customer trust through free burrito offers and other promotions, but these efforts have not fully restored its former popularity. Chipotle’s sales in the first quarter of 2016 fell by nearly 30%, highlighting the severity of the situation.

Moe’s success is partly attributed to its strategic expansion and its ability to adapt to changing consumer preferences. The company opened 70 new restaurants in the past year, contributing to its strong position as a Chipotle alternative. However, to maintain its momentum, Moe’s must continue to convert its brand equity into increased restaurant visits, as noted by David Shim, CEO of Placed Insights.

In conclusion, while Moe’s has made significant strides in the fast-casual Mexican restaurant market, Chipotle still holds a substantial market share and sales advantage. The ongoing competition in the fast-casual sector, with chains like Taco Bell and Qdoba gaining prominence, underscores the need for Moe’s to remain agile and innovative to maintain its position and potentially expand its customer base.

A Delaware family became seriously ill during their vacation at the Sirenusa Condominium Resort in the U.S. Virgin Islands, suspected to have been exposed to methyl bromide, an odorless, potent neurotoxin. The Esmond family, including Steve, Theresa, and their two teenage sons, were airlifted to hospitals after experiencing seizures on March 20. Steve Esmond has regained consciousness, while his sons remain in a critical condition in a coma weeks after the incident. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) confirmed the presence of methyl bromide in the villa where the family stayed, despite the chemical being banned for indoor residential use in 1984. The EPA is investigating the use of the chemical by pest control company Terminix, which has been providing services at the property since late 2013. Terminix is now under criminal investigation by the U.S. Justice Department. Sea Glass Vacations, the rental management company, has terminated its contract with Terminix and is cooperating with authorities. The EPA is also investigating other potential cases of exposure and is working to ensure the chemical is never used improperly again. The use of methyl bromide in the U.S. Virgin Islands highlights the ongoing challenges in enforcing regulations and preventing pesticide misuse, despite the chemical's known dangers.

The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals in Austin, Texas, has upheld key parts of the state's strict anti-abortion law, including hospital-like structural requirements for abortion clinics, which will likely result in the closure of all but seven or eight clinics. This decision follows a second challenge to the 2013 law, which also banned abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy and mandated physicians to have hospital admitting privileges. The structural requirements include specific room and doorway sizes, air sterilization systems, backup generators, and blood supplies, which abortion providers argue are unnecessary and do not enhance patient safety. Prior to the law's passage, there were 40 abortion clinics in Texas; now, only 17 remain, with only seven meeting the building standards. The court made an exception for Whole Woman's Health in McAllen, which will not be required to meet all building requirements or gain admitting privileges for one doctor. The remaining clinics are concentrated in major cities like Austin, Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, and San Antonio, leaving women in more remote areas with limited options. The Center for Reproductive Rights, which sued the state, stated that the decision has the potential to devastate access to reproductive health care on a sweeping scale, not seen since before Roe v. Wade. The ruling is likely to be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, which previously put the law on hold.

Bill Bresnan, a 74-year-old man from Toms River, New Jersey, has been writing his wife Kris a love letter every day since 1974, marking 40 years of marriage. The couple has accumulated over 10,000 cards and notes, which are organized in 25 boxes. Each letter is signed with the phrase "I love you, my darling" and an infinity symbol, reflecting Bresnan's deep commitment to expressing his love daily. Their relationship has been characterized by mutual respect and understanding, with no major fights in their 40-year history. Bresnan attributes their success to working on the relationship daily and never going to bed angry.

Their daily routine includes simple gestures like eating by candlelight, playing games, and having romantic dinners. Bresnan has also taken more significant steps to maintain their relationship, such as reenacting the movie "Summertime" in Venice and even having a friendship ring inscribed with hieroglyphics symbolizing eternal love. Bresnan's daily letters are not just about love but also about documenting their lives together, allowing them to revisit memories and experiences.

Despite their long and successful marriage, Bresnan expresses a fear of forgetting to write his wife a card as he ages. The couple hopes to pass on their relationship advice to younger generations, urging them to prioritize face-to-face interaction and genuine connection over technology. They plan to celebrate Valentine's Day with a simple dinner and a bottle of wine, reflecting their mature and enduring love.

This story highlights the power of daily expressions of love and the importance of maintaining a strong connection in long-term relationships. Bresnan's commitment to writing his wife a card every day serves as a testament to the enduring nature of their love and the value of consistent effort in maintaining a meaningful partnership.

Amanda Longacre, who was stripped of her Miss Delaware title for being too old, has filed a lawsuit against state and national pageant organizations, seeking reinstatement and $3 million in damages. Longacre, who turned 25 after the Miss America pageant deadline, claims she was misled about her eligibility and that other contestants were similarly recruited and disqualified. The lawsuit alleges that pageant officials knowingly recruited ineligible contestants for fundraising and appearances, then disqualified them. Longacre seeks a waiver to compete for Miss America and restoration of her titles and scholarships. The Miss America organization and state pageant officials deny the claims, stating the rules are clear and the case is without merit. Longacre's suit details her extensive efforts and sacrifices made during her reign, including suspending her studies and making numerous public appearances. The case highlights the complexities and controversies surrounding pageant eligibility and the treatment of contestants.

The Arcade Fire's "The Wilderness Downtown" is an interactive website that combines elements of a music video, an interactive film, and a regular website. Visitors are prompted to enter the address of their childhood home, which then triggers a series of multimedia experiences, including videos, animations, and satellite imagery. The website plays the band's single "We Used to Wait" throughout, creating a nostalgic and immersive experience. Created by Radical Media and directed by Chris Milk, the project leverages Google Maps and HTML5 to offer a unique, personalized experience to users. While some may find the concept and execution slightly irritating, the interactive nature of the website could represent a future trend in music video production, moving from traditional television to the internet. The website is optimized for Chrome but works in Safari and other browsers with varying success. For fans of the band, it offers a deeply personal and nostalgic journey through their past.

The investigation into the mass killing of eight members of the Rhoden family in Pike County, Ohio, has entered its fifth day, with authorities finding that seven of the victims were shot multiple times, and some showed signs of struggle before their deaths. The coroner's report indicated that one victim was shot nine times, and soft tissue bruising suggested a struggle. The killings were described as "execution-style" and "pre-planned," with marijuana growing operations discovered at three of the four crime scenes, though a direct link to the murders remains unclear. Authorities have received over 300 tips and are still serving search warrants, with evidence sent to a state crime lab. The Ohio Attorney General's office is leading the investigation, with the FBI and DEA offering assistance. Family members, including Dana Rhoden's father, have expressed disbelief that their loved ones could be involved in illegal activities. A reward of $25,000 has been offered for information leading to the arrest of the suspects.

Google has launched a new wedding planning platform, offering tools for creating wedding websites, editing photos, and planning events through templates in Google Sites, Docs, and Picnik. The initiative, timed for Valentine's Day, includes a collaboration with Michelle Rago, a renowned wedding planner, and features tips for perfect weddings. Google is promoting the service with a $25,000 sweepstakes prize, including Rago's wedding planning expertise. This move is part of Google's strategy to integrate into everyday life, following previous ventures like Google Health, which faced privacy concerns. The new platform aims to provide a seamless experience for couples, blending technology with traditional wedding planning.

MasterCard is expanding its biometric authentication system, allowing customers to use selfies and fingerprints for online payments. The payment processing company has been trialing the system in the U.S. and the Netherlands, with plans to launch it in the U.K. and other European countries this summer. According to Ann Cairns, head of international markets for MasterCard, 92% of test subjects preferred the new system to traditional passwords. The system works by requiring users to download an application to their device, which can then be used to authenticate payments via a selfie or fingerprint scan. To prevent spoofing, users must blink during the selfie process. MasterCard claims that this method is more secure than passwords, which are often weak and reused across multiple sites. The company argues that with the widespread use of smartphones and internet connectivity, biometric authentication is a natural progression. However, security experts caution that biometric data can still be compromised. Despite these concerns, MasterCard asserts that its security measures will prevent or detect suspicious behavior. The move towards biometric authentication is part of a broader trend in the tech industry, with other companies like Alibaba and Microsoft also exploring facial recognition and fingerprint scanning. This shift could potentially reduce fraud and make online payments more secure.

Donald Trump faced criticism after a town hall event where he failed to challenge a questioner's assertion that President Obama is Muslim and that they need to "get rid" of Muslims. Trump's response was seen as inadequate, with advocacy groups and fellow Republicans distancing themselves from him. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest condemned the remarks, and Democratic candidates Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and Martin O'Malley all denounced the comments. Rep. Keith Ellison called it a sign of "a lack of moral courage." The Democratic National Committee Chairwoman, Debbie Wasserman Schultz, flatly called Trump a racist. Trump's campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, later claimed Trump did not hear the question about Obama being a Muslim, instead focusing on training camps. The incident highlights ongoing concerns about Trump's handling of controversial issues and his potential suitability for the presidency.

Ricky Gervais, known for his sharp and often offensive humor, hosted the 73rd annual Golden Globes, delivering a controversial and highly critical monologue that targeted several Hollywood celebrities and industry practices. Gervais began by mocking Sean Penn and Caitlyn Jenner, praising Jenner for her bravery while noting the limited impact on women drivers. He also jabbed at Jennifer Lawrence's push for equal pay, suggesting that her supporters were more concerned with her wealth than her cause. Gervais humorously criticized the nomination of "The Martian" and its director, Matt Damon, and made light of all-female remakes, suggesting they were a money-making scheme for studios.

Gervais took a jab at the Hollywood Foreign Press Association, the organization that hosts the Golden Globes, for their perceived bias and lack of nominations. He also made a pointed comment about Mel Gibson, referencing his infamous 2010 tirade and asking what the phrase "sugar t-ts" meant, which was bleeped by NBC. Gervais also made a joke about Donald Trump, mentioning that Eva Longoria and America Ferrera were people the future president wanted to deport.

In his monologue, Gervais also highlighted the controversy surrounding "The Spotlight" film, which exposed Catholic priests' sexual abuse, and the backlash it received from the Catholic Church. He also made a humorous comment about the 2016 Golden Globes being a comedy, despite "The Martian" being a more enjoyable film than "Pixels." Gervais ended his monologue by warning that the awards were worthless and that no one really cared about them, a statement that was likely meant to provoke thought and discussion.

Gervais' hosting gig was not without controversy, as he had promised to offend Hollywood, and he certainly delivered. His previous hosting experiences, including his 2011 stint, were noted for their controversial nature, with Gervais not afraid to throw shade at celebrities. He had previously hosted the Golden Globes in 2010, 2011, and 2012, and his fourth hosting gig was seen as a significant event in the entertainment industry.

Before the ceremony, Gervais tweeted a shirtless photo with a profane message, warning that he would offend Hollywood. His comments were bold and direct, and he was given free rein by both NBC and the Hollywood Foreign Press Association. Gervais' hosting style, known for its crass and often offensive humor, was a stark contrast to the more traditional and family-friendly approach of previous hosts like Tina Fey and Amy Poehler.

In addition to his hosting duties, Gervais has a rich background in entertainment, having starred in the British version of "The Office" and creating the American version. He has also won a Golden Globe himself, further cementing his status as a significant figure in the entertainment industry. His hosting of the Golden Globes was a significant moment, and his comments, while controversial, generated significant discussion and debate in the entertainment community.

A controversy erupted in Pembroke Pines, Florida, after a police officer was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant due to her being a cop. The manager, Angel Mirabal, reportedly told the officer that the employee "doesn't want to serve you because you are a police officer." The incident sparked outrage and a boycott of the restaurant by law enforcement supporters. The Pembroke Pines Police Department called for an apology and a public statement from Arby's, which CEO Paul Brown provided, stating the behavior was "unacceptable and not representative of the company's values." However, Arby's employees involved, including Kenneth Davenport and his manager, were suspended or fired. The incident led to a national call for a boycott by the police union, with Arby's offering free meals to police officers in South Florida as a gesture of goodwill. Despite the apology, the Arby's manager's grandfather defended his grandson, suggesting the incident was a misunderstanding. The controversy highlights the tension between law enforcement and the business community, with both sides expressing strong opinions on the matter.

Speaker John Boehner has set strict conditions for raising the U.S. debt ceiling, insisting that any deal must include significant entitlement cuts but no tax increases. This stance contrasts with President Obama's call for a "grand bargain" that includes tax hikes. Boehner's comments come after he pulled out of one-on-one talks with Obama, citing disagreements over tax policies and the extent of entitlement reform. He emphasized that the House cannot pass a bill raising taxes on "job creators" and called for a balanced-budget amendment. Despite these disagreements, Boehner acknowledged that the two parties must work together to avoid a government default, though he believes the White House is not fully committed to the necessary entitlement reforms. The upcoming White House meeting aims to finalize a deal before the Aug. 2 deadline, but the impasse over tax hikes and entitlement cuts remains a significant hurdle.

During a House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology hearing, Rep. Mo Brooks (R-Ala.) challenged the consensus view that global warming is causing sea levels to rise, instead proposing alternative explanations. Brooks argued that erosion, silt deposition from major rivers, and the physical displacement of water by cliffs like the White Cliffs of Dover could be significant contributors to rising sea levels. He cited the Mississippi, Amazon, and Nile rivers as examples, and even suggested that the Antarctic ice sheet was growing, contrary to scientific evidence.

Philip Duffy, president of the Woods Hole Research Center, countered that these factors were negligible on human timescales and that satellite records showed a clear shrinkage of the Antarctic ice sheet. Brooks, however, maintained that NASA data in his district contradicted this, and he cited studies showing Antarctic ice growth. His comments were widely reported and criticized for their scientific inaccuracies.

Brooks' skepticism about climate change is not new; he has previously expressed doubts about the consensus view on climate change, attributing past climate scares to cooling concerns in the 1960s and 1970s. He suggested that many climate scientists lack the long-term data needed to make accurate predictions and that their conclusions are influenced by financial interests and political motivations.

The hearing and Brooks' comments drew significant media attention and criticism for their scientific inaccuracies. The committee later tweeted a link to an op-ed denying climate change's role in sea-level rise, further highlighting the tension between scientific consensus and political skepticism.

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid and Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell have made significant progress in negotiations with the White House to reach a deal on raising the debt ceiling. The talks, which began late Saturday night, have been ongoing, with both sides working to finalize the details. Key issues include the requirement for "dollar-for-dollar" deficit reductions and the enforcement mechanism for a joint committee to achieve $1.6 trillion in savings. Boehner has insisted on these terms, while the White House has been resistant, particularly regarding the potential for across-the-board cuts, including deep defense cuts.

Despite the progress, there are still concerns among Democrats, particularly Reid, who expressed skepticism about McConnell's commitment to the process. Boehner, meanwhile, has shown signs of running out the clock, hoping for concessions from the White House. The Senate failed to break the 60-vote threshold to end debate on Reid's bill to raise the debt ceiling by $2.2 trillion, with a vote of 59-41. The House is expected to vote on the deal tonight, with Reid hopeful of a vote but acknowledging that significant elements still need to be finalized.

The negotiations are critical as the Treasury warns of potential default if a deal is not reached by the deadline. Both sides are working to ensure that any agreement is robust enough to prevent future crises while also addressing their respective priorities. The outcome of these negotiations will have far-reaching implications for the U.S. economy and political landscape.

New Zealand is considering significant hikes in cigarette prices to reduce smoking, aiming for a smoke-free nation by 2025. Health Ministry officials propose prices could rise to $100 per packet, though this is deemed unrealistic. The government is also exploring other measures like regulating tobacco as a toxic substance, banning smoking in cars with children, and doubling anti-smoking campaigns. However, Prime Minister John Key warns such drastic price increases could fuel a black market. The Associate Health Minister, Tariana Turia, supports whatever it takes to achieve the smoke-free goal. The Ministry acknowledges these are policy discussions and not final decisions.

Giant hogweed, an invasive plant species native to the Caucasus region, has been discovered for the first time in Clarke County, Virginia. This plant is highly toxic, causing severe burns and even blindness when its sap comes into contact with skin and is exposed to sunlight. The sap contains photosensitizing furanocoumarins, leading to phytophotodermatitis, which results in painful blisters, long-term sun sensitivity, and potential scarring that can last up to six years. Environmental officials warn residents to be vigilant and avoid using weed-whackers, as the sap can splatter and spread quickly. For eradication, manual removal or herbicides like glyphosate or triclopyr are recommended. Long-term monitoring is crucial, as seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 15 years. Giant hogweed can grow up to 14 feet tall, creating shade and inhibiting native species growth. The plant is also found in other states, such as New York, where control methods involve root cutting, flower head removal, and repeated herbicide applications. Proper safety measures, including protective clothing and avoiding direct sunlight, are essential when handling the plant.

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), the auditing firm responsible for handling the Oscars votes, issued a statement taking full responsibility for the Best Picture flub at the 89th Academy Awards. According to PwC, their partner Brian Cullinan mistakenly handed the Best Actress envelope to Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway, leading to the incorrect announcement of La La Land as the Best Picture winner. In their statement, PwC acknowledged that their protocols were not followed quickly enough to correct the mistake, and they expressed gratitude for the graciousness shown by the involved parties, including the presenters and the casts of La La Land and Moonlight.

PwC's U.S. chairman and senior partner, Tim Ryan, stated that the firm and its partners, including Cullinan, felt very bad about the mix-up. The company also faced scrutiny over Cullinan's social media activity, as he posted a photo of Emma Stone backstage just minutes before the Best Picture announcement, despite being instructed not to use social media during the show. This incident, along with the mix-up, could potentially impact PwC's 83-year relationship with the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

Following the incident, the Academy launched a full-scale review of its relationship with PwC. One proposed change is to station two auditors at each stage entrance instead of one on each side, to act as a fail-safe and prevent similar mistakes. The review also includes an examination of the Emma Stone tweet posted by Cullinan, to determine if it violated any policies. The incident has highlighted the need for stricter protocols and oversight to ensure the integrity of the Oscars voting process.

A music enthusiast named Craig Mandell has launched a crowdfunding campaign on Tilt to prevent the Canadian band Nickelback, led by Chad Kroeger, from performing in London. Mandell's initiative, titled "Don't Let Nickel Back," aims to raise $1000 (£626) to ensure the band does not schedule any gigs in the city. The campaign encourages contributors to send emails to Nickelback's management, with the severity of the message depending on the donation amount. For instance, a $1 donation results in one email, a $5 donation leads to a "slightly more forceful email," and a $50 donation includes an email with an attached mp3 of Nickelback's music, potentially leading to the band's retirement. Mandell envisions a scenario where thousands of music lovers in London do not witness an exclusive Nickelback concert, which he believes would be "glorious."

The campaign is not for personal gain, as Mandell states that all proceeds will go to charity or therapy for those affected by the band. As of the original article's writing, no funds had been raised, and the deadline was set for November 3. Meanwhile, a similar campaign to bring the Foo Fighters to Cornwall has already surpassed its £150,000 target in just two days, though it now faces the challenge of convincing the band to agree to a performance in the county.

Interestingly, the original article mistakenly identified the crowdfunding platform as Kickstarter, but it was actually Tilt. This campaign is part of a trend where fans use crowdfunding to influence their favorite bands, whether to bring them to a city or, in this case, to keep them away.

"True Grit," a Coen brothers' adaptation of Charles Portis' novel, stars Jeff Bridges as U.S. Marshal Rooster Cogburn, who is hired by 14-year-old Mattie Ross to find her father's killer, Tom Chaney. The film, shot in a classic Western style, features Matt Damon as a Texas Ranger and Josh Brolin as Chaney. Roger Deakins' cinematography enhances the film's poetic and haunting atmosphere. While Bridges' portrayal of Rooster is nuanced and compelling, the film also includes a preening Texas Ranger and a scarred thug, creating a mix of humor and drama. The Coens' faithful adaptation, with a strong performance by Hailee Steinfeld as Mattie, delivers a wonderfully entertaining and visually stunning Western that pays homage to the genre while offering fresh perspectives.

Rhonda Thill, whose husband Randy was killed in a motorcycle accident, was devastated to lose his wedding ring. The ring, which Randy wore for nearly 19 years, was not among the personal effects returned to her by authorities. Despite several attempts by friends and family to locate the ring, including a metal detector search, it remained missing. 

Tim Allen, a high school friend of Rhonda, reached out to the towing company that had Randy's motorcycle. Allen then coordinated a search involving members of the Sober Soldiers motorcycle club. The group, led by Jay Stevens, followed the tow truck to the crash site and began a thorough search. After persistent digging, Stevens found the ring pushed into the soil behind a weed.

The discovery was a profound moment for Rhonda, who was overwhelmed with emotion. She later expressed gratitude for the kindness of the strangers who helped her find the ring, saying, "He just had to make a call, and all those people have such kind hearts. They didn't hesitate."

The story culminates with a benefit event, "Riding with Randy," which will take place on September 5, 2014, at the St. Paul Saloon. This event aims to honor Randy and raise funds for Rhonda and her children.

The Bracamontes, a family in Upland, California, are dealing with a live-in nanny, Diane Stretton, who has refused to leave their home after being fired. The situation has garnered national attention, with Stretton's belongings still in her room and her presence spotted by media outside the house. According to the Bracamontes, Stretton stopped working and refused to vacate the premises, leading them to fire her on June 6. However, Stretton claims she was never terminated and has demanded certain conditions for her departure, including the absence of media and a delay due to the upcoming heat wave. She has agreed to leave by July 4, but the Bracamontes are skeptical, fearing Stretton might use the delay as a tactic to remain in the house.

The family has plans to be away for a family wedding on July 2, but Marcella Bracamonte intends to have family members house-sitting to ensure Stretton does not gain unauthorized access. Stretton's past has come to light, revealing a history of legal issues, including being listed as a vexatious litigant in California. She has been involved in numerous lawsuits, often against her own family members, and has even sued a car rental agency for property damage and personal injury.

The Bracamontes have expressed concerns about potential legal repercussions if they interfere with Stretton's room, as she was provided a room in exchange for her services. They also face the possibility of fines if they disrupt her living conditions, as the laws regarding the housing agreement differ from those governing the employment arrangement. The situation highlights the complexities and legal challenges faced by families in such domestic disputes, especially when dealing with a live-in caregiver who refuses to leave.

A federal judge temporarily blocked the deportation of Pablo Villavicencio, a 35-year-old Ecuadorean restaurant worker, after he was arrested while making a delivery to Fort Hamilton in Brooklyn. Villavicencio, who has two young U.S.-born daughters and is married to an American citizen, was ordered to leave the U.S. in 2010 but stayed. A routine background check revealed an active warrant for his deportation. The Legal Aid Society obtained a temporary stay until July 20, 2018, through a habeas corpus petition. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, a Democrat, called for an investigation into ICE conduct and requested Villavicencio's release, citing his long-term residency and contributions to the community. Villavicencio's attorney argued that the arrest and detention were hasty and cruel, emphasizing the need for a fair judicial process. The case highlights the complexities and potential injustices in the U.S. immigration system, particularly for those with pending applications for legal status.

"The Big C," a Showtime series starring Laura Linney, explores the life of a high school teacher diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma. Linney's character, Cathy, initially keeps her diagnosis secret and embraces a more carefree and unconventional lifestyle, much to the dismay of her husband, Paul, and son, Adam. While the show attempts to be a dark comedy, it often falls flat due to over-the-top character portrayals and a lack of nuance. Linney's performance, however, is commendable, and the show has potential. The series aims to challenge the viewer's perception of how one should live when facing a terminal illness, but the execution is inconsistent. Despite some promising moments, the show's reliance on broad humor and unrealistic character dynamics hinders its effectiveness. Overall, "The Big C" struggles to balance its serious subject matter with comedic elements, resulting in a mixed reception.

In the early morning of Wednesday, a tragic altercation over a prized fighting rooster led to the death of Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, and left his nephew, Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., 28, hospitalized. The rooster, named "Bubba," was found tied to a chair outside the trailer, unharmed. Timothy Johnson confronted Larry, accusing him of stealing the rooster, which Larry denied. The confrontation escalated into a shootout, with Larry Johnson shooting his uncle four times. Larry Johnson was flown to the University of Tennessee Medical Center in critical condition, while Timothy Johnson's body was taken for an autopsy. The case remains under investigation, with toxicology results and an investigative file to be reviewed by the Meigs County Grand Jury in November. Both families expressed shock and regret over the incident, emphasizing that it should not have escalated to such violence.

The case of 17-year-old Kendrick Johnson, who died in a gym at Lowndes County High School in January, has taken a disturbing turn with the discovery that his organs were removed and his body stuffed with newspaper before burial. This revelation has intensified the Johnsons' skepticism of the initial conclusion that Kendrick's death was accidental. The state medical examiners had ruled that Johnson suffocated after getting stuck in a rolled-up gym mat while reaching for a sneaker. However, a private autopsy by Dr. Bill Anderson found that Kendrick had sustained a blow to the right side of his neck, suggesting non-accidental, blunt force trauma. 

The Johnsons, after winning a court order, had Kendrick's body exhumed and a second autopsy performed. During this process, Anderson discovered that all of Kendrick's organs, including the brain, heart, lungs, and liver, were missing, leading to questions about who might have taken them. The Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) and the Harrington Funeral Home have been implicated in the handling of the body. The GBI stated that the organs were returned to the body after the initial autopsy, while the funeral home claimed they were destroyed due to the body's position at death.

Death scene imagery obtained by CNN has raised further suspicions of foul play, with a former FBI agent, Harold Copus, suggesting that Kendrick's death was not accidental. The sheriff's department has closed the case, but federal prosecutors in south Georgia are reviewing the evidence and considering whether to open their own investigation. The Johnsons remain convinced that their son was murdered, and the macabre discovery of his body has only deepened their belief. 

The case highlights the ongoing struggle for justice and the importance of thorough investigations, especially in cases where the initial findings are questionable. The family's determination to uncover the truth and the potential for a new investigation underscore the complexity and sensitivity of such cases.

President Obama demanded that House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid work out a budget deal or face daily meetings at the White House until an agreement is reached. Obama, after a meeting with Boehner and Reid, stated that the White House team is prepared to meet for as long as necessary to resolve the issue, warning that a failure to act would be inexcusable. Boehner's office denied that he excluded the White House from the discussions. The meeting did not produce an agreement, and Boehner proposed a one-week extension with $12 billion in spending cuts, which Obama rejected. The situation looms over the possibility of a government shutdown, with both sides accusing each other of pushing for harmful spending cuts and attaching policy riders. Additionally, the House has proposed long-term budget deficit reduction plans, including a controversial Medicare reform.

President Donald Trump's tweet about the London subway attack, which stated that the perpetrators had been "in the sights of Scotland Yard," drew criticism from British officials, including Prime Minister Theresa May. May condemned Trump's rhetoric, emphasizing that the police and security services were working to uncover the full circumstances of the attack and identify all responsible parties. Trump's tweet was part of a broader series of comments that included calls for tougher measures against "loser terrorists" and a suggestion to cut off their internet access, which serves as a recruiting tool for terrorists.

National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster attempted to clarify Trump's statement, indicating that the president was speaking generally about Scotland Yard and that law enforcement is focused on the threat of terrorism. However, this did not mollify British officials, who have a history of tension with the Trump administration over issues such as intelligence sharing.

The tweet also drew comparisons to Trump's previous statements, particularly his criticism of the Obama administration's approach to fighting terrorism. In response, Trump claimed that the U.S. had made more progress against ISIS in the past nine months than the Obama administration had in eight years. This claim was made in the context of a broader call for increased toughness and proactiveness in the fight against terrorism.

The diplomatic fallout from Trump's comments threatened to strain the special relationship between the U.K. and the U.S., especially given the ongoing intelligence sharing issues. Trump later issued a statement expressing sympathy for the victims and pledging continued collaboration with the U.K. to combat terrorism. He also used the opportunity to criticize the Obama administration and to tout U.S. military capabilities in response to both terrorism and the recent North Korean nuclear test.

Despite the tensions, Trump and May spoke about the North Korean situation, agreeing that China must use its leverage to bring pressure to bear on North Korea to end its illegal nuclear tests. The tweet also reignited the debate over Trump's controversial travel ban on people from predominantly Muslim countries entering the U.S.

The Great Recession significantly impacted American retirement plans, with approximately 40% of individuals aged 45 and over delaying their retirement. This shift affects various aspects of American society, including Social Security, financial markets, and workforce demographics. The report from the Federal Reserve highlights that only 25% of individuals actively plan for their retirement, with a concerning 31% of respondents having no money saved for retirement. Among those nearing retirement age, 19% have zero savings. The majority of respondents rely on Social Security as their primary source of income in retirement, with 33% of those surveyed delaying their retirement date. Additionally, 44% of respondents use a 401(k) or 403(b) as their primary savings vehicle. The report also indicates that 54% of individuals with incomes under $25,000 have no retirement savings or pension, compared to only 10% of those earning $100,000 or more. The findings underscore the uneven nature of the economic recovery, with 68% of families reporting being the same or worse off financially compared to 2008. The survey reveals that 34% of respondents are doing "somewhat or much worse" than in 2008, highlighting the persistent financial struggles of many Americans.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old "Modern Family" star, has been in the spotlight for her candid social media presence and fearless approach to fashion. Known for posting scantily clad photos and maintaining a "zero-fucks-given" attitude, Winter recently faced backlash for her choice of attire at a Modern Family event. During an appearance on Conan's show, she inadvertently used a baby voice, which garnered widespread criticism. Despite this, Winter remains unapologetic about her choices, emphasizing the importance of self-acceptance and self-expression. In a social media post, she defended her decision to wear a glamorous dress, stating, "Why do I have to be like everyone else? Why can’t people just let other people feel good about themselves and do what they want?" Winter's stance aligns with her broader message of empowering young women and men to embrace their individuality. While her baby voice garnered negative attention, her commitment to self-love and authenticity continues to resonate with many fans.

Japanese author Haruki Murakami, known for his surreal and often philosophical works, is set to engage with readers through a unique online column. Murakami, who is notoriously reclusive and has previously joked about biting fans, will answer questions from readers on his publisher's website, "Murakami's Place," from January 15 to 31. His responses will be published until the end of March, offering insights into his thoughts and interests, including his passion for running, cats, and baseball. This project, which echoes a similar 2006 initiative, provides a rare opportunity for fans to communicate directly with the author, who is a perennial contender for the Nobel Prize in Literature.

Born in Kyoto, Murakami's novels, translated into over 50 languages, explore the absurdity and loneliness of modern life. His latest novel, "Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage," was an instant bestseller in Japan. The publisher expects a mix of serious and unconventional questions, with Murakami's responses depending on his interest. The column is part of a broader effort to engage with readers, as Murakami stated, "After so long, I want to exchange emails with readers."

The column is part of a series of literary pieces, including poems and prose, that explore various themes and emotions. Clive James's poem "Fred" reflects on the elegance and grace of dance, while "The Glen" by Kathleen Jamie captures the serene beauty of a Scottish landscape. Other works, such as "The Adulteress" by Kathryn Maris and "Words" by Patrick Daly, delve into personal and abstract themes, reflecting the diverse range of contemporary literature.

This engagement with readers not only highlights Murakami's enduring popularity but also underscores the evolving relationship between authors and their audience in the digital age.

President Obama's recent decision to launch airstrikes against the Islamic State and Al Qaeda's Khorasan Group in Syria marks a significant shift in U.S. strategy, raising questions about the extent of the military commitment and the potential for a prolonged air campaign in a country that did not invite intervention. This move comes after Obama had previously resisted involvement in Syria's civil war, citing the complex and unstable nature of the conflict's factions. The decision was influenced by the rapid advance of Islamic State fighters in Iraq, their brutal treatment of civilians, and the beheadings of American journalists, which prompted Obama to promise a long-term campaign to degrade and ultimately destroy the Islamic State.

The airstrikes, which also targeted the Khorasan Group, represent a major reversal for Obama, who had previously opposed any significant U.S. military engagement in Syria. This shift has led to concerns about the potential escalation of U.S. involvement, including the possibility of deploying ground forces. General Martin Dempsey, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, has already indicated a willingness to recommend the deployment of U.S. military "advisors" to accompany Iraqi troops into battle, suggesting that the situation may require a more direct military presence.

While the airstrikes are seen as a necessary response to the immediate threat posed by the Islamic State, critics argue that the case for an ever-escalating U.S. military role in Syria and Iraq has yet to be fully made. The primary concerns revolve around the clarity of the strategy and the achievable aims. The airstrikes are intended to stop ISIS assaults on Kurdish civilians and to target the Khorasan Group, but the broader implications and potential long-term consequences of this intervention remain uncertain.

The decision to involve the U.S. military in Syria also highlights the complex and interconnected nature of the conflicts in the Middle East. The U.S. must navigate the delicate balance between addressing immediate threats and avoiding the pitfalls of prolonged military engagements, which can have unintended and far-reaching consequences. As the situation continues to evolve, it will be crucial for the U.S. to maintain a clear and strategic approach to ensure that any military intervention aligns with broader national interests and objectives.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in a death penalty case involving Ronald Mikos, a convicted killer in Illinois whose lawyers argued prosecutors improperly used his silence as evidence of lack of remorse. Mikos, a former foot doctor, was sentenced to death for the 2005 murder of a disabled nurse, Joyce Brannon, to prevent her from testifying against him in a Medicare fraud trial. The 7th Circuit Court upheld the sentence. Meanwhile, federal prosecutors announced they would seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping, torturing, and killing visiting scholar Yingying Zhang in June 2017. The case highlights the rare use of the death penalty in federal courts, with the last execution in Illinois being that of Ronald Mikos in 2005. Christensen's case involves allegations of a 2013 sexual assault and additional victims, and his trial is likely to be delayed due to the lengthy process. The announcement marks the third time in recent weeks that U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions has opted to pursue the death penalty.

Wal-Mart de Mexico is under scrutiny for alleged bribery to secure construction permits, with the U.S. Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission investigating potential violations of the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA). According to The New York Times, Wal-Mart paid over $24 million in bribes, and when whistleblowers alerted top executives in 2005, the company failed to report the findings to law enforcement. The revelations have tarnished Wal-Mart’s image, which had been improving after facing criticism for low wages and small business competition. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, which has ties to Wal-Mart, has been advocating for the FCPA to be scaled back. Wal-Mart’s shares fell nearly 5% following the news, and the company faces calls for executive departures and increased scrutiny. The investigation could slow Wal-Mart’s expansion in Mexico and other markets, and penalties could be substantial if the allegations are proven. The company maintains that the incidents are not reflective of its values and is conducting its own investigation.

A tragic incident unfolded in Sparks, Nevada, involving a couple who were featured on the reality TV show "Ghost Adventures." Mark and Debby Constantino, both paranormal investigators, were found dead in an apartment near Sparks High School, after a standoff with police. The couple had been in a contentious relationship, with Debby obtaining a restraining order against her estranged husband and they were scheduled to appear in court regarding their pending divorce. The incident began when Reno police received a call about a man found dead in a northwest Reno home. They tracked Debby Constantino's cellphone to an apartment in Sparks, where they found her with her husband. Upon arrival, officers heard several shots and negotiations ensued, eventually leading to the use of explosives to breach the door. Inside, they found the couple dead. The cause of death was not immediately released. The couple had a history of domestic issues, with Debby being a victim of a previous kidnapping and domestic incident. The incident also involved the lockdown of Sparks High School as a precaution. The case remains under investigation, with no other suspects identified.

"Sparkle," a remake of the 1976 musical starring Irene Cara, was released just months before Whitney Houston's death, making it a bittersweet and often cringe-inducing experience. Houston's performance, particularly in a powerful church scene, is a highlight, but the film struggles with its narrative and dialogue, often feeling like a straightforward Supremes biopic with clichéd plot points. The film follows three sisters—Sister, Dolores, and Sparkle—who form a girl group in 1960s Detroit. Houston plays their mother, a former singer who turned to substance abuse before finding God. While the film attempts to capture the spirit of the era, it is criticized for its cardboard dialogue, predictable plot, and underdeveloped characters. Jordin Sparks, the American Idol winner, plays Sparkle, but her performance is lackluster. Carmen Ejogo, however, delivers a strong and dynamic performance as Sister. The film's most memorable moments are the musical numbers, particularly Houston's powerful rendition of "His Eye Is on the Sparrow." Despite its flaws, "Sparkle" serves as a poignant tribute to Houston, offering a final glimpse of her onscreen presence.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative icon and the court's longest-serving justice, was found dead at a ranch in West Texas on February 13, 2016, at the age of 79. His death sparked immediate political debate over whether President Obama should nominate a replacement. Obama announced his intention to do so, but Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell argued that the nomination should wait until after the next presidential election. Scalia's death had significant implications for the court, particularly in cases awaiting decisions. He was known for his originalist approach to the Constitution, his sharp wit, and his conservative views on issues such as abortion, affirmative action, and gun rights. His passing also led to a flurry of statements from political figures and legal experts, with many praising his contributions to legal thought and lamenting his loss. The vacancy created by Scalia's death could significantly impact the balance of the court, especially in a presidential election year.

A Catholic priest in the Philippines faced disciplinary action after he used a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass, an incident that went viral and drew criticism from his diocese. The priest, whose identity was not disclosed, was seen riding the hoverboard up and down the nave of his church, singing "May the Good Lord Bless and Keep You." When he concluded his impromptu performance by delivering the final blessing, parishioners applauded. However, the Diocese of San Pablo was not pleased with the priest's actions, stating that it was inappropriate to introduce such an activity during the Mass, which they emphasized is the church's highest form of worship, not a personal celebration.

The diocese issued a statement announcing that the priest would be suspended and would spend time reflecting on the incident. The priest acknowledged his mistake, apologized, and promised that such an occurrence would not happen again. This suspension serves as a "wake-up call" for the priest, according to the diocese. The incident highlights the strict adherence to traditional practices within the Catholic Church and the potential consequences for deviation from established norms.

The use of hoverboards as Christmas gifts was a popular trend in 2015, despite the risks associated with their use. The priest's case underscores the importance of maintaining decorum and respect for religious traditions, even in the face of modern technological advancements.

On a Saturday night, a 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, fell from a stopped gondola ride at Six Flags Amusement Park in Queensbury, New York. The incident occurred just after 8 p.m., with the girl falling about 25 feet from a stationary two-person car on the "Sky Ride" attraction. The ride was promptly stopped by an operator upon receiving word of a rider in distress.

The teenager struck a tree before landing in a crowd of park guests and employees, who had gathered to try to catch her. She was initially treated by park emergency medical staff and then transferred to Glen Falls Hospital via ambulance before being airlifted to Albany Medical Center, where she was reported to be in stable condition with no serious injuries.

An investigation revealed that the ride was in proper working order, and the park stated that the safety of guests is a top priority. As a precaution, the "Sky Ride" was closed until a thorough review could be completed. Additionally, an unidentified 47-year-old man from Schenectady, who was also a park guest, sustained a back injury while attempting to catch the falling girl. He was treated and released from the hospital.

The Warren County Sheriff's Office conducted the investigation and confirmed that the ride did not malfunction. The park's statement emphasized their commitment to guest safety and the need for a comprehensive review of the incident.

This incident highlights the importance of safety measures in amusement parks and the potential risks associated with such attractions. The swift response from the park and the medical staff ensured that the girl received immediate care, and the closure of the ride until a thorough review underscores the seriousness of the situation.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his 2010 and 2011 tax returns, revealing a lower effective tax rate of 13.9% for 2010 and 15.4% for 2011, compared to the top wage-earner tax rate of 35%. Romney's income primarily comes from investment profits, dividends, and interest, with his 2010 income totaling $42.5 million and his 2011 estimated income at $42.2 million. He paid $6.2 million in taxes in 2010 and expects to pay $3.2 million in 2011.

The release of Romney's tax returns coincided with President Barack Obama's State of the Union address, where he proposed the "Buffett rule" to ensure the ultra-wealthy pay their "fair share" of taxes. Romney's tax returns also showed he had $13 million in "carried interest" income, taxed at 15%, and significant charitable contributions, including $4.1 million to the Mormon Church.

Romney did not release tax returns from 1984 to 1999, the years he built his fortune at Bain Capital. The returns also revealed Romney's holdings in Cayman Islands and Swiss bank accounts, which he claimed were fully taxed. Romney's tax rate is lower than that of President Obama and his Republican rival, Newt Gingrich, raising questions about the fairness of the tax code and income inequality.

The release of Romney's tax returns came after his loss in the South Carolina primary to Gingrich, who questioned Romney's financial transparency. Romney's campaign hopes the release will help him regain momentum, but Democrats argue for more transparency, calling for 12 years of tax returns. The issue of "carried interest" and the tax treatment of investment income versus wages is likely to be a contentious topic in the upcoming election.

On May 1, 2017, SpaceX successfully launched a Falcon 9 rocket from Kennedy Space Center, Florida, carrying a classified National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) mission labeled NROL-76. The launch faced initial challenges due to high-altitude winds, but SpaceX proceeded, landing the first stage rocket at Landing Zone 1 for potential reuse. This mission marked SpaceX's first dedicated launch for the NRO and was crucial for the company's efforts to secure government contracts. The rocket's performance and trajectory led amateur satellite observers to speculate that the payload might be an imaging satellite, possibly replacing a 2006 satellite that failed. The launch was SpaceX's fifth of the year, following a period of grounding due to a launch pad explosion. SpaceX has now achieved 10 rocket landings, with plans to expand its reusable rocket capabilities, aiming to reduce launch costs significantly and support future missions, including potential Mars colonization efforts.

In 1996, Alexa Internet began donating their web crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This data has been invaluable for preserving the internet's history. Recently, Josh Duggar, a former star of the reality TV show "19 Kids and Counting," was sued by Matthew McCarthy, who claims his face was used without permission on Duggar's Ashley Madison and other dating profiles. McCarthy, a DJ and photographer, feels humiliated by the connection to Duggar's past and is seeking damages. Duggar's OkCupid profile, which was later removed, had a username matching his alleged Ashley Madison account, "joesmithsonnwa," and featured a photo of Matthew McCarthy. The profile's details, such as the user's occupation and salary, raised suspicions of a connection to Duggar. However, the profile's deletion and the lack of definitive evidence prevent a clear link. The incident highlights the ongoing scrutiny and legal challenges faced by Duggar following his child molestation scandal.

UC Irvine (UCI) faced significant backlash after rescinding admission offers to 499 students due to issues with transcripts and grades, contributing to a higher-than-expected acceptance rate. Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs, Thomas Parham, acknowledged the university's "harder line" on terms and conditions and apologized for any perceived mistreatment. The university initially planned to admit 6,250 freshmen but received over 104,000 applications, leading to a more stringent admissions process.

Parham's letter addressed the concerns of affected students and their parents, emphasizing that all students meeting the terms and conditions would be welcomed. However, the university's approach drew criticism, with some students and their families alleging mistakes in the application process. For instance, Johnny Wang, a high school graduate with a 4.3 GPA, had his offer rescinded due to a missing transcript, despite evidence that his transcript was sent via certified mail. Simran Chopra, another student, locked herself in a bathroom and cried after learning her admission was revoked, despite believing she had submitted all required documents.

The university has since expedited the appeal process, with 63 students already reinstated. UCI has pledged to correct any errors swiftly and provide support to affected students. Despite these efforts, some students, like Julia Kim, have decided to attend other institutions, such as Clark University, due to the uncertainty and anxiety caused by the admissions process. The incident highlights the challenges universities face in managing high application volumes and the potential impact of stringent admissions criteria on student morale and future enrollment.

The scandal involving former CIA Director David Petraeus has expanded to include Marine General John Allen, the U.S. commander in Afghanistan. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) investigation into Petraeus's communications revealed that Allen, who is now under scrutiny, exchanged numerous emails with Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite. Kelley had previously complained to the FBI about receiving harassing emails, which led to the investigation. The emails between Kelley and Allen, both married, were discovered after the investigation began focusing on Broadwell, Petraeus's biographer and alleged mistress. 

Defense Secretary Leon Panetta asked the Senate to put on hold Allen's confirmation as NATO commander, pending the investigation. Allen has denied any affair with Kelley or sharing any classified information. The emails between the two, dating back to 2010, are currently under review, and no evidence of criminal wrongdoing or security lapses has been found. Allen remains commander of the International Security Assistance Force in Afghanistan while the facts are ascertained.

Jill Kelley, who is also an honorary consul of South Korea, invoked her honorary diplomatic status in a 911 call, claiming inviolability of her property. However, this title does not provide actual legal protection. Court documents reveal that the Kelleys, who hosted top military brass, are in significant debt, with multiple properties in foreclosure. Jill's twin sister, Natalie Khawam, is also in financial trouble, having filed for bankruptcy due to over $3 million in debt, much of it related to a loan from the Kelleys.

The scandal has raised questions about the extent of Kelley's influence and the nature of her interactions with military officials. While Allen's nomination as NATO commander may yet proceed, the investigation is ongoing, and the outcome remains uncertain.

Hollywood legend Tony Curtis, who passed away from cardiac arrest at 85, disinherited his five children, including actress Jamie Lee Curtis, in his last will and testament. The will, written five months before his death, acknowledged his children but stated that he had intentionally chosen not to provide for them. Instead, his estate was left to his widow, Jill Vandenberg Curtis. One of the children contested the will but was unsuccessful. Jamie Lee Curtis, who eulogized her father at his funeral, and her siblings now find themselves excluded from their father's will. Jill Curtis stated that her husband's wishes are private family matters.

The Tice family, along with the families of other American hostages killed by the Islamic State, have issued a joint letter to President Obama, urging the administration to use all necessary means to find and return missing U.S. journalist Austin Tice. Tice, who was last seen in August 2012, has been held captive by unknown gunmen for over four years. The families of the slain hostages, including James Foley, Steven Sotloff, Abdul-Rahman Peter Kassig, and Kayla Mueller, have united in their plea, highlighting the urgency of the situation and the potential steps the administration could take. 

The letter emphasizes the administration's responsibility to act boldly and without hesitation, despite potential political concerns. It also underscores the families' frustration with the Obama administration's handling of the situation, particularly the lack of acknowledgment of Tice's case during the White House Correspondents Association dinner. 

The Tices have been working with the families of the slain hostages to advocate for changes in hostage policy and have expressed their commitment to maintaining hope for their son's safe return. The families of the deceased hostages have used their personal testimonies to emphasize the gravity of the situation and the need for immediate action. 

Austin Tice, the only American journalist being held captive in the world, remains in unknown custody. His case has garnered attention from the highest levels of the U.S. government, but the families are urging the administration to do more. The letter concludes by acknowledging the Tice family's unwavering hope and the need for the government to maintain its commitment to finding and bringing Tice home.

A video game allowing players to simulate a school shooting was set to release on Steam, but Valve Corporation removed it after controversy. The game, "Active Shooter," developed by Revived Games and published by ACID, faced backlash from survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting and politicians. Valve found the developer, Ata Berdiyev, to be a "troll" with a history of abuse and manipulation. The game offered players the choice to play as a shooter or a SWAT team member, with a score counter tracking civilian and police kills. Critics argued that the game was inexcusable and profited off tragedy. This incident highlights the ongoing debate over the ethics of violent video games, with many calling for stricter content policies.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., has set a firm stance on the border wall issue, stating that she will not trade her support for the wall with President Donald Trump. Pelosi described the wall as a "manhood issue" for the president, emphasizing that Democrats support border security but prefer to focus on strengthening existing measures as part of a comprehensive immigration overhaul. Pelosi's comments come as the issue is expected to be a significant point of contention in December, when appropriations negotiations are set to resume. While the House Republicans are likely to pass the $5 billion Trump requested for the wall, Senate Democrats, led by Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, could pose a significant obstacle. Pelosi's stance on the wall could shift if Democrats win the House majority in the upcoming midterm elections, as she has stated that she would be ready to challenge for the position of Speaker if Democrats take control. Pelosi also discussed Democrats' priorities for the next year, which include lowering healthcare costs, increasing paychecks, and improving green infrastructure. She emphasized the importance of campaign finance reform as the first bill of the new Congress. Regarding oversight, Pelosi stated that impeachment is not a path she wants to pursue, but Democrats will hold the Trump administration accountable in a thoughtful manner.

The 2014 All-Star Game at Target Field in Minneapolis was a celebration of Derek Jeter, with Adam Wainwright, the National League starting pitcher, playing a significant role. Wainwright's gesture of stepping back to let Jeter have a moment before the game was well-received, but his candid comments after the game quickly turned controversial. Wainwright admitted to planning to give Jeter a "pipe shot," which was perceived as disrespectful by some, despite Jeter's own dismissive response.

The incident highlighted the complex issues surrounding the "This One Counts" initiative, which links the All-Star Game's outcome to the World Series home-field advantage. This system has faced criticism for complicating the game's traditional format and diluting its entertainment value. The voting process, involving fans, players, and managers, has also been criticized for its lack of clarity and fairness.

Wainwright's comments were seen as a breach of etiquette, but his intention was to show respect and appreciation for Jeter's career. However, his candor backfired, leading to a public relations nightmare. Wainwright's self-criticism and regret underscored the pressure he felt to balance respect and competition.

The controversy also raised questions about the All-Star Game's purpose. While the game has become a significant event, the "This One Counts" initiative has outlived its usefulness. The game should focus more on entertainment and fan engagement rather than being a high-stakes event. This incident could serve as a catalyst for MLB to reassess the All-Star Game format and its role in the broader baseball landscape.

In conclusion, while Wainwright's comments were poorly timed, they brought to light the complexities and controversies surrounding the All-Star Game. The incident could potentially lead to positive changes, making the game more enjoyable and less contentious for all involved.

On June 14, 2016, a Chinese national was fined $1,000 and a $30 court processing fee for walking off the boardwalk in the Mammoth Hot Springs thermal area of Yellowstone National Park. The incident was reported by a visitor who observed the individual breaking through the fragile travertine crust and collecting thermal water, likely for medicinal purposes. The Chinese tourist admitted to not reading the safety information provided at the park entrance. A federal violation notice was issued, requiring the man to appear in the Yellowstone Justice Center Court.

This case follows a series of incidents at Yellowstone, including the death of 23-year-old Colin Nathaniel Scott, who fell into a hot spring on June 7, 2016. The park has emphasized the importance of staying on designated trails and boardwalks for both visitor safety and the protection of natural resources. Regulations prohibit the collection of park resources, and violations can result in significant fines. Park officials urge visitors to comply with these rules to prevent further damage to the park's unique features and to avoid potential harm to themselves.

The betel nut, a seed from the Areca catechu palm, has been a long-standing tradition in many Asian cultures, providing a stimulating effect similar to six cups of coffee.
