A hostage crisis at an Algerian gas facility, involving militants and foreign workers, ended with Algerian forces killing 23 hostages and 32 militants in a final assault. The attack, lasting three days, resulted in at least 55 deaths, including those of two Americans. The militants, linked to Al-Qaeda, targeted the facility to pressure France, which had used Algerian airspace to attack Islamist militants in Mali. The operation highlights the ongoing threat of terrorism in North Africa and the need for international cooperation. While some hostages were freed, the fate of several remains unknown, including five Norwegians, five British nationals, and 14 Japanese. The crisis underscores the balance between security and economic interests in Algeria, a major gas producer.

The New Orleans Times-Picayune, one of the oldest newspapers in America, is cutting its print edition to three days a week—Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday—while ramping up its online presence. This move is part of a broader strategy by Advance Publications, the paper's owner, to transition to a digital-first model. The decision comes as the newspaper industry faces a crisis of declining readership, advertising, and profits. While the Times-Picayune will maintain 24/7 online reporting via its site, Nola.com, the reduced print schedule reflects the industry's struggle to balance the high costs of print production with the lower revenue from digital platforms.

The cuts will affect the newsroom, with an estimated 50 journalists losing their jobs, leaving about 100 to cover a region of 1.2 million people. This reduction in staffing raises concerns about the quality and depth of local journalism. The paper's history includes significant contributions, such as its coverage during Hurricane Katrina, which earned it a Pulitzer Prize. Despite these challenges, Advance Publications believes that combining the award-winning journalism of the Times-Picayune with the strength of Nola.com will help it succeed in the digital age. However, the transition is risky, and it remains uncertain whether the new model will be sustainable or if it will lead to further declines in readership and advertising.

Two years ago, Ellen Martinsen, a research associate at the Smithsonian's Conservation Biology Institute and adjunct faculty in the University of Vermont's biology department, discovered a previously unknown malaria parasite, Plasmodium odocoilei, in white-tailed deer while collecting mosquitoes at the Smithsonian's National Zoo. This discovery was significant as it was the first-ever malaria parasite found in a deer species and the only native malaria parasite found in any mammal in North or South America. Martinsen and her colleagues estimate that the parasite infects up to 25% of white-tailed deer along the East Coast of the United States.

The discovery was made by chance when Martinsen was looking for malaria that might infect birds. The parasite was identified using advanced DNA technology, specifically polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technology, which amplifies DNA to make it easier to study. The team screened more than 300 white-tailed deer and found 41 animals harboring the parasite, with 25% of the animals tested at sites in Virginia and West Virginia carrying the parasite. No infected deer were identified in the west, but the parasite was widespread in the east.

The new findings challenge the previous understanding that malaria parasites in mammals originated in the Old World, mainly Africa and Asia. The researchers suggest that the malaria parasites have a long evolutionary history in the New World, dating back to the ancestors of white-tailed deer that made their way to the continent across the Bering Land Bridge 2.3 million to 6 million years ago. This discovery marks the first finding of a malaria parasite species of mammals that is native to the Americas.

Despite the widespread presence of the parasite, scientists are quick to note that there is little danger to people from this newly discovered deer malaria. However, the discovery underscores the importance of understanding the biology of other species, as many human health concerns are connected to wider ecological systems. The findings also raise questions about whether the parasite might infect other species, such as dairy cows or other hoofed animals.

The study was a collaboration with scientists from the Smithsonian Conservation Biology Institute, the American Museum of Natural History, the National Park Service, the University of Georgia, the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, and UVM biologist and malaria expert Joseph Schall. The research highlights the importance of parasite surveys and basic natural history, as well as the potential for malaria to have a low-level burden that could hurt deer populations.

In conclusion, the discovery of Plasmodium odocoilei in white-tailed deer not only reshapes our understanding of malaria's origins but also emphasizes the need for further research to determine the impact of the parasite on deer populations and whether it might infect other species. This finding underscores the importance of continued ecological and biological research to better understand the diversity and distribution of malaria parasites across different species.

In June 2014, a Wal-Mart truck driver, Kevin Roper, who had been awake for 28 hours, caused a crash that severely injured comedian Tracy Morgan and killed another comedian, James McNair, after hitting a limo carrying Morgan and others from behind on the New Jersey Turnpike. Roper had driven 800 miles overnight from Georgia to Delaware, and his decision contributed to the crash. The truck was traveling at 65 mph, 20 mph over the 45 mph speed limit, and could have stopped before impact if it had been traveling at the posted speed limit. The limo passengers, including Morgan, were not wearing seat belts, which exacerbated their injuries. The crash involved 21 people in six vehicles, and it took 37 minutes for emergency responders to extricate some of the victims from the limo. Roper was charged with vehicular homicide and assault by auto but pleaded not guilty. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) criticized Wal-Mart for not having a comprehensive fatigue management program and recommended improvements. Wal-Mart later took steps to educate drivers about fatigue and implement a program to reduce it. The crash highlighted the dangers of driver fatigue and the importance of seat belt use.

A study by University College London suggests that alcohol consumption in England may be significantly higher than previously thought, with almost half of alcohol sold unaccounted for in consumption surveys. This discrepancy implies that as many as three-quarters of people may be drinking above the recommended daily alcohol limit. The researchers used alcohol sales data from Revenue and Customs and compared it with self-reporting surveys from 2008, finding that 19% more men and 26% more women were exceeding daily limits, and 15% more men and 11% more women were exceeding weekly limits. The study highlights that irregular and chaotic drinking behavior, such as mixing drinks and drinking at different venues, may contribute to underreporting. The researchers recommend that government drinking guidelines should reflect actual consumption to better assess harmful levels. The Department of Health acknowledges the issue and is considering changes, while Diane Abbott MP calls for more action to address problem drinking, which costs the country £21 billion.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has expanded its recommendation for Zika virus screening in blood donations to all states and territories, not just areas with active transmission. This change follows the first locally acquired Zika cases in the continental U.S., reported in Miami-Dade and Palm Beach counties. Florida Surgeon General Celeste Philip stated that the state's blood collection centers have been testing donations since August, and expanding this practice makes sense given the prevalence of the Aedes aegypti mosquito. The FDA's decision is based on the potential severe health impacts of Zika, particularly on pregnant women and their unborn children. While there have been no confirmed cases of Zika transmission through blood transfusions in the U.S., the agency emphasizes the precautionary nature of the new policy. The expansion will be phased, with 11 states starting testing within four weeks, and all states expected to be fully compliant within 12 weeks. The move reflects the evolving understanding of Zika's transmission and the potential risks it poses, especially in light of the virus's spread to new regions.

Lindsey Buckingham, a key member of Fleetwood Mac, has settled a civil lawsuit against his former bandmates after being removed from a 2018/19 tour. The effectiveness of the Club for Growth's ad campaign remains to be seen, as Trump has survived similar attacks before. However, the campaign is likely to intensify the ongoing battle for control of the Republican Party's economic orthodoxy and could potentially impact Trump's lead in the polls.

Scientists have discovered a new species of centipede, *Geophilus hadesi*, in the Velebit Mountains of Croatia, which lives in the deepest known cave habitat of any centipede, nearly 1 kilometer below the Earth's surface. This unique species, named after the Greek god of the underworld, Hades, is one of only two geophilomorph centipedes known to spend their entire lives in caves, the other being *Geophilus persephones*, named after the queen of the underworld, Persephone. The centipede's adaptation to the dark, underground environment is evident in its elongated antennae and fur-like setae, which help it detect prey in complete darkness. 

*G. hadesi* feeds on various small invertebrates, including larvae, springtails, worms, and spiders, and its venomous bite is harmless to humans. The centipede's long, flattened body and thin claws allow it to navigate the rocky crevices of its habitat. The researchers suggest that the species' adaptation to cave life may be due to a change in external conditions, forcing less-adaptive organisms to seek more stable underground environments. The Velebit Mountains are known for their subterranean biodiversity, and the discovery of *G. hadesi* highlights the potential for many more undiscovered species in the region.

The centipede's habitat extends to depths of 3,609 feet (1,100 meters), making it the deepest known centipede habitat. This discovery adds to the growing list of pale, cave-dwelling creatures in the Velebit Mountains, which are part of the Dinaric Karst, a hotspot for subterranean diversity. The lead author, Pavel Stoev, notes that the discovery underscores the limited knowledge of life in caves, even in well-explored areas, and the potential for finding more incredible animals in these environments.

Researchers from the University of Florida have confirmed the first known case of a human infected with the Keystone virus, a mosquito-borne illness previously found in animal populations along coastal regions stretching from Texas to the Chesapeake Bay. The virus was first identified in 1964 in Keystone, Florida, but its presence in humans was unknown until a 16-year-old boy in North Central Florida sought treatment for a fever and severe rash in August 2016, during the Zika outbreak. Despite initial tests for Zika and other pathogens, the virus was only identified after a year and a half of intensive laboratory work. The virus, carried by the Aedes atlanticus mosquito, a cousin to the Zika-spreading Aedes aegypti, can cause mild symptoms such as a rash and fever, and may pose a risk for brain infections. The researchers suspect that the infection may be fairly common in North Florida, with a 1972 study indicating that 19 to 21 percent of people tested in the Tampa Bay region had antibodies to the virus. The University of Florida is now working with biotech companies to develop commercial tests for the virus, emphasizing the need for further research into vector-borne diseases in the United States. The findings highlight the ongoing threat of mosquito-borne illnesses and the importance of continued surveillance and public health measures.

A study from Imperial College London and Instituto de Investigaciones Biomédicas ‘Alberto Sols’ explored how fiber fermentation affects appetite, focusing on acetate, a short-chain fatty acid. Mice were fed either a high-fat diet with inulin (HF-I) or cellulose (HF-C) as a control. Acetate was found to accumulate in the hypothalamus, a brain region that controls appetite, and was metabolized via the glutamine-glutamate cycle, potentially suppressing appetite. Mice on the HF-I diet consumed less food and weighed less than those on the HF-C diet.

Acetate was also detected in serum and feces, and its effects were confirmed through PET-CT scans and direct injection into the bloodstream, colon, or brain of mice. Acetate injections reduced food intake, suggesting its potential as a weight management tool. However, critics argue that the high fiber levels used in the study might have caused discomfort, and that the mechanism of acetate's effect on appetite is overly simplistic.

The researchers believe this mechanism could apply to humans, as acetate is known to be metabolized in the human brain and gut bacteria can produce it from fiber. They are developing methods to deliver acetate in nanoparticle form to mimic its slow release and suppress appetite. This could lead to new non-invasive treatments for obesity, though challenges remain in ensuring the acetate pill is both effective and safe for human use.

The researchers concluded that raw milk failed to reduce lactose malabsorption or symptoms among adults with lactose malabsorption. This finding challenges the widespread claim that raw milk offers benefits for those with lactose intolerance. The study highlights the need for further research to explore other potential health benefits of raw milk, if any exist. Additionally, the article discusses the genetic basis of lactose intolerance, noting that it is more common in certain populations, such as Asian-Americans and African-Americans, and less common in northern Europeans. It also mentions that while there are no serious health consequences of lactose intolerance, alternative sources of calcium and lactose-free products are available for those who cannot tolerate lactose.

This study, published in Nature Neuroscience, examined brain changes in women before and after their first pregnancy by comparing MRI scans of 25 primiparous women with 20 nulliparous women who did not become pregnant. Key findings include:

1. **Brain Volume Changes**: The study identified 11 brain regions showing reduced gray matter volume in the post-pregnancy women compared to the control group. These changes were consistent and detectable by a computer program analyzing MRI scans.

2. **Persistence of Changes**: The brain changes were still present two years after childbirth, as assessed in 11 of the original participants.

3. **Specific to Motherhood**: No brain changes were observed in first-time fathers, suggesting these changes are specific to pregnancy and motherhood.

4. **Hormonal Influence**: The researchers hypothesize that the brain changes are due to increased sex hormones during pregnancy, which may lead to the pruning of synapses, a process that can occur during adolescence to enhance brain efficiency.

5. **Potential Functional Benefits**: The affected brain areas overlap with regions involved in understanding others' thoughts and feelings, which could be beneficial for motherhood.

6. **No Cognitive Decline**: The women showed no signs of cognitive decline, as evidenced by memory tests.

The study's authors suggest that these brain changes may prepare women for motherhood by enhancing their ability to understand and respond to their infants' needs. Future research is needed to understand the exact mechanisms and potential long-term impacts of these changes.

The case highlights the issue of untested rape kits, a problem that has affected many jurisdictions. In 2015, Seattle Police Chief Kathleen O'Toole initiated an initiative to test each of the backlogged kits. At the time, only 365 out of 1,641 rape kits administered in the previous 10 years had been tested. This initiative, prompted by the DNA match in the Bolar case, underscores the importance of testing all rape kits to ensure justice for victims and to prevent future crimes.

The case also brings attention to the broader issue of rape kit backlogs. In Washington, the Attorney General's office received a $3 million grant from the U.S. Department of Justice to test and investigate the 6,460 untested rape kits stored at law enforcement agencies throughout the state. While only 25 percent of the grant had been used to inventory the backlog, the office announced plans to request the remainder to facilitate the testing and investigation of these kits.

This case serves as a stark reminder of the long-term impact of untested rape kits and the critical need for prompt and thorough investigation of sexual assault cases.

Justin Bieber's arrest for DUI and resisting arrest in Miami Beach has led to a series of peculiar developments, including a video showing him doing 23 1/2 pushups in 28 seconds while in jail. The video, obtained by TMZ, showcases Bieber's physical fitness, though it's unclear why he chose to demonstrate it. Law enforcement reports indicate that there is one part of the 9-hour video where Bieber is clearly under the influence, but the video itself does not appear to show this.

Another interesting aspect of the case involves the difficulty law enforcement has had in blurring Bieber's genital area in the jailhouse videos. The Miami Beach police are struggling to obscure his private parts as he urinates, leading to technical challenges. The judge has ordered the release of the remaining videos, but with sensitive portions blacked out to protect Bieber's privacy.

In a related development, Miami-Dade County Judge William Altfield ruled that two of the five unreleased video clips depict Bieber's genitalia during a drug test. The judge agreed with Bieber's legal team that the videos should be released with sensitive portions redacted, prioritizing Bieber's right to privacy. The remaining three clips, which are too far away to discern details, will be released without any redactions.

The still photos released by the Miami Beach Police Department show close-ups of Bieber's numerous tattoos, including a praying Jesus, a grinning joker's face, and an Indian chief's head. These images were taken shortly after his arrest and provide a glimpse into his personal style.

Bieber has pleaded not guilty to the charges of driving under the influence, resisting arrest, and driving with an expired license. The case continues to unfold, with a trial date yet to be set.

This document describes a collaborative project aimed at documenting and preserving the federal government's web presence by archiving government websites and data. Key partners include the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative and the Data Refuge project. The project extends the 2016 End of Term project, ensuring ongoing archiving of publicly nominated websites beyond the official end of the previous project. Interested members of the public, particularly government information specialists, are invited to submit selected websites for inclusion using a public nomination tool.

The document also details a significant policy move by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) to implement a nationwide smoking ban in public housing units. HUD's proposed rule would require more than 3,100 public housing agencies to design policies prohibiting lit tobacco products in all living units, indoor common areas, administrative offices, and outdoor areas near housing and administrative office buildings. HUD Secretary Julián Castro cited the health benefits of the ban, including protecting residents from secondhand smoke and saving $153 million annually in healthcare, repairs, and preventable fires.

The ban is part of a long-standing effort to reduce smoking, which has been linked to numerous health issues. HUD's encouragement of anti-smoking policies since 2009 has already resulted in more than 228,000 smoke-free units. However, concerns remain about enforcement, particularly regarding residents' personal space and freedom. Housing authority officials and legal experts have raised questions about how the ban will be implemented, especially for elderly and disabled tenants who may struggle with the new rules.

The ban is expected to improve public health by eliminating exposure to secondhand smoke, but it also faces challenges in enforcement and may create hardships for some tenants. The document concludes by noting the ongoing efforts by the U.S. surgeon general's office to address smoking's health impacts and the economic benefits of the ban, including reduced damage and maintenance costs associated with smoking.

A powerful hailstorm struck the Cheyenne Mountain Zoo in Colorado Springs, damaging buildings and habitats, and injuring 14 people. The storm, which included hail the size of golf balls, killed two animals—a 13-year-old caped vulture and a 4-year-old Muscovy duck—and severely injured a third vulture. The zoo was evacuated, and visitors were transported to Cheyenne Mountain High School. Nine people were treated on-site, and five were taken to the hospital. The zoo will be closed Tuesday for repairs. The storm also affected nearby areas, including the Broadmoor Hotel, and caused power outages and road closures. Forecasters warned of potential flooding due to heavy rain and runoff.

Nicki Minaj, the "MotorSport" rapper, has donated $25,000 to Geoffrey Owens, a former actor from The Cosby Show who was shamed for working at Trader Joe's. Minaj, who was upset by the internet backlash against Owens, felt compelled to help him. She expressed that Owens is a "whole f**king legend in these streets" and hoped to personally reach out to him. Owens, 57, had been working at Trader Joe's for 15 months to maintain flexibility in his acting career. The situation gained widespread attention after a photo of him working was published, leading to a backlash from some outlets and individuals. However, the incident also sparked a wave of support and encouragement from celebrities and fans. Tyler Perry, for instance, offered Owens a role in an OWN drama series, which Owens accepted, agreeing to a recurring role in 10 episodes of "The Haves and the Have Nots." Owens, who played Elvin Tibideaux on The Cosby Show from 1985 to 1992, initially felt humiliated but ultimately saw the situation as a blessing, noting that it has brought him many job offers and support. He also expressed gratitude to his son for his understanding during the ordeal. Despite the initial shock and hurt, Owens maintained a positive outlook, emphasizing the importance of perseverance in his industry.

Rep. Trent Franks (R-Ariz.) expressed a controversial wish that another armed individual was present during the Tucson shooting to potentially stop Jared Lee Loughner. This sentiment aligns with arguments from other Republicans, like Rep. Steve King (R-Iowa), who also believe more firearms could enhance security. However, the effectiveness of such measures is questionable, as evidenced by the case of Joe Zamudio, an untrained individual who managed to subdue the shooter by chance. The discussion of increased security measures includes calls for better coordination between lawmakers and local law enforcement, with some representatives, like Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah), planning to carry concealed weapons. Overall, the debate highlights the complex balance between security and potential risks associated with widespread gun ownership.

The massive $1.3 trillion government spending bill, which ended budget battles and averted a federal shutdown, has been approved by Congress. The bipartisan legislation, which funds the government through September, includes significant funding for both military and domestic programs. The bill was passed by the House with a 256-167 vote, reflecting its popularity. However, Senate passage was delayed due to conservative objections, particularly over provisions related to Democratic priorities. A late-night procedural issue involving a provision to rename a forest in Idaho further delayed the Senate vote. Once resolved, the Senate approved the bill with a 65-32 vote. The bill's passage was a relief to both parties, avoiding a third federal shutdown this year. Despite the compromise, the bill's size and scope have stirred conservative opposition and set the stage for future budget battles. The legislation includes funding for military increases, border wall construction, and programs like child care development and fighting the opioid crisis. However, it also marks a return to $1 trillion deficits, a significant shift for Republicans who campaigned on spending restraints. President Trump, while reluctant, ultimately supported the bill, acknowledging the need for necessary trade-offs to secure Democratic votes. The bill's passage highlights the entrenched divisions within the Republican Party, making leadership's job of controlling the majority challenging. Democrats, while pleased with the outcome, faced their own internal divisions, particularly regarding the fate of young Dreamer immigrants. The bill's approval underscores the complex political landscape in Congress and the difficulty of achieving bipartisan agreement on major legislation.

The launch of the Healthcare.gov website, a cornerstone of the Affordable Care Act, faced significant technical challenges, leading to a crisis that threatened President Obama's presidency. Despite initial claims that the site would be as simple as shopping on Kayak or Amazon, the website's functionality was severely compromised, causing widespread frustration and a decline in public approval ratings for both the law and the administration. The failure was attributed to several factors, including an insular White House that downplayed potential issues and CMS's decision to handle the systems integration in-house, which proved inadequate.

The selection of CGI Federal, a Canadian company, as the lead contractor for the project was scrutinized, with some suggesting it was due to political connections rather than technical expertise. However, internal documents show that the decision was based on a "technically superior" proposal, despite CGI Federal's history of troubled projects, including the AMS failure. The CMS's use of pre-qualified contractors from a 2007 umbrella contract, which included CGI Federal, further complicated the selection process. 

Despite the initial success in recent weeks, the website continues to face issues, including errors in enrollment records. CGI Federal remains involved in the project, working to improve system performance and user experience. The controversy surrounding CGI Federal highlights the challenges of federal government contracting, particularly in technology projects, where specialized expertise is often lacking, and the selection process can be influenced by factors beyond technical merit.

The U.S. State Department issued a global travel alert on August 30, 2014, warning of potential al Qaeda attacks in the Middle East, North Africa, and beyond, citing specific and worsening intelligence. The threat is particularly concerning for Yemen, where the U.S. Embassy is under heightened scrutiny. The alert prompted the temporary closure of 21 embassies and consulates, including those in Afghanistan, Algeria, Bahrain, and Iraq. The threat is described as more specific than previous ones, with al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula reportedly in the final stages of planning an unspecified attack, possibly timed to coincide with Laylet al-Qadr, a significant Muslim holiday.

The travel alert and embassy closures are seen as a proactive measure to protect U.S. citizens and interests, with bipartisan support from U.S. officials. The decision to close embassies is seen as prudent, given the history of attacks on U.S. diplomatic missions in the region. The alert comes amid ongoing investigations into the September 11, 2012, attack on the U.S. consulate in Benghazi, Libya, which killed four Americans, including Ambassador Christopher Stevens. The alert and closures are intended to provide an "abundance of caution" and prevent potential attacks, as emphasized by Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Gen. Martin Dempsey.

A new spider genus and species, Trogloraptor marchingtoni, has been discovered and described in the journal Zookeys. This spider, which forms the basis of a new family, Trogloraptoridae, was found in the Klamath-Siskiyou region of Oregon and California, specifically in caves and old-growth forest understory. The spider is about the size of a half-dollar coin and is characterized by its large raptorial claws, suggesting it is a fierce predator. Despite its discovery, many aspects of Trogloraptor's biology remain unknown, including its mating habits and diet. Only a dozen specimens have been collected, and the spiders were found hanging from silk strands on cave roofs. The discovery of Trogloraptor, which has unique features suggesting an ancient lineage, may lead to revisions in the understanding of spider evolution. The Klamath-Siskiyou region is known for its ancient species, and the discovery of Trogloraptor hints at the possibility of more undiscovered species in the area.

On India's Independence Day, three people, including two children, died after their throats were slit by glass-coated kite strings, known as manja. Saanchi Goyal (3), Harry (4), and Zafar Khan (22) were among the victims. These strings, used to cut competitors' kites, also injure and kill hundreds of birds annually. The Delhi government has banned the use of sharp manja and promised educational campaigns. Authorities will prohibit the sale, production, and storage of such strings, imposing penalties and jail terms for violations. Animal rights group PETA also petitioned for a ban, citing serious injuries and fatalities to both humans and birds.

A new study from the London School of Economics, analyzing data from the Millennium Cohort Study, suggests that women in their 30s are more likely to give birth to smarter and healthier babies compared to those in their 20s or 40s. The study, published in the journal Biodemography and Social Biology, found that children born to mothers in their 30s scored higher in cognitive testing and exhibited better overall development. This trend is attributed to several factors: older mothers are more likely to be educated, have higher incomes, be in stable relationships, have healthier lifestyles, seek prenatal care earlier, and plan their pregnancies.

The research also indicates that women in their 40s, while less likely to smoke and more likely to breastfeed and read to their children, are more prone to having obese children due to their reduced likelihood of playing with their kids. The average age of mothers in the UK has been steadily increasing, from 24.5 in 1980 to 28.1 today.

However, the study's findings are not without criticism. Some argue that intelligence is multifaceted and not solely determined by maternal age or socioeconomic status. The study's conclusions may be influenced by the socio-economic advantages that typically come with older age, such as better education and financial stability. Critics also point out that the study's sample size for mothers in their 40s was relatively small, comprising only 53 participants, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.

Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable insights into the relationship between maternal age and child development, suggesting that women who are in their 30s when they have their first child may experience certain advantages in terms of their child's cognitive development and overall health.

In 1996, Alexa Internet began donating their web crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This data has been crucial for preserving the internet's history. A case study published in the BMJ medical journal details an incident where an 18-year-old man, thought to have appendicitis, was actually suffering from severe liver injuries sustained from a paintball game. The patient was admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain, fever, and a lack of appetite, symptoms consistent with appendicitis. However, during surgery, doctors discovered that the liver was the source of the problem, with a laceration causing internal bleeding. The patient had been hit twice in the abdomen during a paintball game two days prior, though he had not informed the medical staff of this incident. Doctors were surprised by the severity of the liver injury, as it was the first reported case of paintball-related liver damage. Paintball pellets, traveling at velocities of 100 to 300 feet per second, can cause significant harm, including ocular and intra-abdominal injuries. The patient required multiple operations to stop the bleeding, and three weeks later, he returned with an ultrasound showing residual blood in the liver. However, the bleeding had stopped, and the liver was functioning well. This case highlights the potential for seemingly minor incidents to result in severe internal injuries and underscores the importance of thorough patient histories in diagnosing conditions.

Michael Oreskes, the chief of NPR's newsroom, has resigned following accusations of sexual harassment dating back to the 1990s. Oreskes, who previously served as a vice president and senior managing editor at The Associated Press, was placed on leave by NPR President and CEO Jarl Mohn after The Washington Post reported on two women who claimed Oreskes kissed them without their consent during job discussions. The women, who spoke on condition of anonymity, alleged that Oreskes initiated these kisses while they were discussing their career prospects with him in the 1990s, when he was the Washington bureau chief at The New York Times. In a statement, Oreskes expressed deep regret for his actions, acknowledging that his behavior was wrong and inexcusable.

Oreskes' behavior was not limited to these incidents. A current NPR employee, Rebecca Hersher, also came forward with an account of an uncomfortable dinner meeting with Oreskes in 2015. During a career counseling session, Oreskes extended an invitation to dinner, which turned into a three-hour-long discussion that delved into personal matters, including relationships and sex. Hersher felt the conversation devalued her as a professional and reported the incident to NPR's human resources division. NPR rebuked Oreskes, and Hersher felt the network had handled the situation appropriately.

Following the new allegations, Mohn appointed Chris Turpin as the temporary news chief. In a statement, Mohn encouraged employees to come forward if they have experienced harassment, emphasizing NPR's commitment to a safe and productive work environment. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges in addressing and preventing sexual harassment in the workplace, even among high-ranking executives.

Elisabeth Hasselbeck, a co-host on The View, sparked controversy by suggesting that older lesbians are a product of men's preference for younger partners, leaving older women with no male options. This view drew criticism from her co-host Joy Behar, who argued that being gay involves more than just sexual attraction. Hasselbeck's comments followed a pattern of controversial statements, including her previous sexist remarks about Erin Andrews and her stance on the morning-after pill. Behar and others on the show denounced Hasselbeck's logic, emphasizing the complexity of sexual orientation and the societal pressures that can influence personal choices.

Myanmar's government is releasing 73 political prisoners, with more expected to be freed in the coming months to honor commitments made by President Thein Sein during his recent trip to Europe. Thein Sein, a former general now leading a quasi-civilian government, has initiated a series of political and economic reforms since the military government stepped aside in 2011. He has freed hundreds of political detainees and pledged to release all remaining prisoners by the end of the year. The Committee to Scrutinise Remaining Political Prisoners, a 19-member body comprising 10 former political prisoners, six government-appointed individuals, and three mediators, is overseeing the process. The government's figures for the number of political detainees differ from those of pro-democracy activist groups. While the release of political prisoners is seen as a positive step, concerns remain about the continued incarceration of activists and the presence of repressive laws. Activists note that scores of peaceful protesters are still being arrested and tried. Overall, the release of these prisoners marks a significant step in Myanmar's transition towards a more open and democratic society, though challenges remain.

In a bizarre incident, a pair of Chow Chow dogs were seized from a circus in Brescia, Italy, after being painted and dyed to resemble pandas, tricking visitors into paying for photo opportunities. The dogs, originally from Hungary, were reportedly in good health but suffered from watery eyes, possibly due to frequent exposure to camera flashes. The circus, run by Riccardo Gravina, denied any cruelty, stating the dogs were treated like children. However, the animals are now returned, and the circus is barred from using them in shows. The incident highlights a shift in Chinese attitudes towards dogs, where they are now seen as companions rather than food, as reported by Hsin Ch’en, a pet shop owner in Sichuan. The dogs were seized on animal cruelty grounds, as their passports were falsified, and the circus owner faces charges for potentially cheating customers. This case underscores the ethical concerns surrounding the use of animals in entertainment and the changing cultural perceptions of pets.

Nolan Daniels, a Facebook user, claimed to be the second winner of the $588 million Powerball lottery and offered to give $1 million to a random person who shared his winning ticket photo. The photo, which Daniels posted late Thursday, showed him holding a ticket with the winning numbers, but the ticket has not been publicly verified. Daniels also suggested that anyone doubting the legitimacy of the photo would not be included in the $1 million drawing. The post quickly went viral, with the photo being shared over 200,000 times. However, the numbers on Daniels' ticket were not in numerical order, which is a requirement for a valid Powerball ticket. The official Powerball FAQ states that the white ball numbers are printed in numerical order. The other winner, who bought a ticket in Arizona, has not come forward. The payout is the second largest in US history, after three ticket buyers shared a $656 million jackpot in March. The growing frenzy over Daniels' claim highlights the gullibility of social media users and the potential for such posts to go viral regardless of their authenticity.

Construction workers in Gdansk, Poland, have unearthed a marble bust of Adolf Hitler, created by Josef Thorak, one of the Third Reich's official sculptors. The bust, measuring 50 cm (20 inches) in height, was found buried in the garden of the National Museum in Gdansk. The sculpture bears the inscription "Thorak 1942," indicating its creation date and the artist's name. Lech Lopuski, a curator at the museum, suggests that the bust was likely hidden in 1945 as the Soviet army approached the city. The museum curator notes that the sculpture was buried about 60 cm underground to avoid destruction, despite repeated attempts to install a fountain and flower beds over the years.

The museum currently has no plans to display the bust, as it needs to be scientifically studied to determine its provenance, original location, and how it ended up in the museum. Thorak's sculptures were often monumental, designed to adorn official buildings and public spaces. In May 2023, two 33-foot-long bronze horse statues, which had stood outside Hitler's chancellery in Berlin, were recovered by German police, having been missing since 1989.

Josef Thorak's works were widely used to decorate government buildings and public spaces during the Nazi era. His sculptures often depicted military and government themes, as well as heroic and nude figures. The bust of Hitler, along with other sculptures by Thorak, provides a glimpse into the propaganda and art of the Third Reich. The discovery of the bust in Gdansk highlights the ongoing efforts to uncover and preserve historical artifacts from this period, while also raising questions about their future display and interpretation.

NPR has terminated the contract of Juan Williams, a long-time news analyst and commentator on Fox News, following his comments on the Fox program "The O'Reilly Factor" where he expressed nervousness when seeing people in Muslim dress on airplanes. Williams argued that his comments were not bigoted but rather a reflection of his personal experience post-9/11. NPR CEO Vivian Schiller stated that Williams' controversial opinions should not come from NPR reporters and that his views on Muslims should be kept private. Republicans criticized NPR's decision, with former House Speaker Newt Gingrich calling for an investigation into potential censorship. Williams, who has written extensively on race and civil rights, defended his comments, stating that he meant what he said and that his firing was an assault on free speech. Fox News subsequently signed Williams to a new multi-year contract, with him writing columns for FoxNews.com. The controversy highlights the tension between media outlets and the challenges of maintaining journalistic integrity while addressing sensitive issues.

Katherine Heigl, the once-popular rom-com queen, has returned to the entertainment industry with a new TV show, "State of Affairs," and an animated film, "The Nut Job." She took a break from Hollywood in 2009 to focus on her family and career reevaluation. Heigl admitted she overdid romantic comedies and needed to diversify her roles. She believes taking time off helped her find a better work-life balance and reignite her creativity. Heigl's return to Los Angeles is marked by a more balanced career, with a deal to limit her TV show's episodes to 15 per season, allowing her to return to Utah and pursue other interests. She still has a connection to Hollywood, but her current focus is on her new projects and personal growth.

In a separate piece, the rocky on-screen relationship between Ryan Gosling and Rachel McAdams during the filming of "The Notebook" is revealed. Gosling reportedly wanted McAdams removed from the set, citing creative differences. However, the tension between the two was resolved through a shouting match. Gosling later admitted that he and McAdams inspired the worst in each other during the film's production. Despite their on-screen conflict, the two eventually developed a real-life romance, dating on and off until 2007. Gosling humorously described their breakup as a "draw," indicating a mutual agreement to end their relationship. This story highlights the stark contrast between the idealized romances portrayed in films and the often messy realities of real-life relationships.

A powerful storm system, fueled by the remnants of Hurricane Patricia, hit Texas, causing significant flooding and disruptions. In Navarro County, a freight train derailed due to floodwaters, with two crew members rescued after swimming to high ground. The train remained overturned, and authorities awaited receding waters to attempt recovery. In San Antonio, a man was swept away while walking his dog, and a dog was found safe, but the man's search was suspended due to severe weather. Heavy rainfall in the region, reaching up to 21 inches in 24 hours, triggered 72 swift water rescues. Major highways, including Interstate 45, were closed, leading to traffic backups. The remnants of Patricia, now a tropical depression, are expected to exacerbate the flooding, with 8 to 10 inches of rain predicted for Houston. Galveston County issued a voluntary evacuation for Bolivar Peninsula, anticipating 8 to 12 inches of rain and high tides. Other cities like Austin, San Antonio, and Corpus Christi also faced flash flood watches. Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport experienced 100 flight cancellations, and the airport recorded a daily rainfall record of 3.24 inches. The storm's impact is expected to linger through at least Monday, with potential coastal flooding concerns in some areas.

Sen. Bernie Sanders is introducing a "Medicare for All" bill in the Senate, marking a significant shift in the U.S. health care debate. This proposal aims to transition the U.S. to a single-payer health care system, where a government-run plan would provide health coverage to all Americans. Here are the key points:

### 1. **Scope and Benefits of the Plan**
- **Universal Coverage**: The plan would cover all American residents in one government-run health plan.
- **Generous Benefits**: It would include hospital visits, primary care, medical devices, lab services, maternity care, and prescription drugs, as well as vision and dental benefits.
- **No Out-of-Pocket Costs**: Unlike other single-payer systems, it would cover all services fully, with no copayments or deductibles.

### 2. **Financing and Implementation**
- **Financing**: The plan does not specify how to finance such a generous benefit package. Sanders promised to release a set of financing options later.
- **Transition Period**: The plan would be phased in over four years, starting with Medicare benefits for children and gradually lowering the eligibility age.
- **Phased Implementation**: By the fourth year, everyone would be eligible for the universal Medicare plan.

### 3. **Support and Opposition**
- **Support**: The bill has gained support from 11 Senate Democrats, including Kamala Harris, Elizabeth Warren, Cory Booker, and Kirsten Gillibrand.
- **Opposition**: Notable Democrats like Chuck Schumer, Sherrod Brown, and Dianne Feinstein have not endorsed the bill.
- **Political Pressure**: The bill is seen as a litmus test for potential 2020 Democratic nominees, with support from key figures like Harris, Warren, and Booker.

### 4. **Public Support**
- **Growing Popularity**: A June 2017 Pew Research Center survey found that 60% of Americans support the idea of the federal government ensuring health care coverage for all.
- **Intra-Party Competition**: The push for Medicare for All is seen as a way to attract liberal voters and activists, potentially shaping the 2020 Democratic primary.

### 5. **Economic and Political Considerations**
- **Cost and Taxation**: The plan would likely require significant tax increases, particularly on the wealthy, to fund the program.
- **Political Feasibility**: While the bill faces strong opposition from Republicans, Democrats are divided on the issue, with some fearing alienating moderate voters.
- **Long-Term Goals**: The introduction of the bill is seen as a long-term strategy to shift the Democratic Party's focus to the left, potentially making it the party's defining issue.

### 6. **Impact on Current Health Care System**
- **Transition**: The plan would gradually phase out private insurance, with a four-year transition period.
- **Administrative Efficiency**: It aims to reduce administrative costs by consolidating billing to a single government entity.
- **Potential for Higher Spending**: The generous benefits and lack of out-of-pocket costs could lead to increased health care utilization, potentially raising overall health care spending.

### 7. **Broader Political Context**
- **2020 Nomination Race**: The push for Medicare for All is seen as a way to attract progressive voters and activists, potentially shaping the 2020 Democratic primary.
- **Intra-Party Dynamics**: The bill is seen as a way to unite the party's left wing and potentially shift the party's platform to the left.

### 8. **Public and Political Reactions**
- **Support from Activists**: The introduction of the bill is seen as a victory for progressive activists who have long advocated for a single-payer system.
- **Mixed Reactions Among Democrats**: While some see it as a way to attract liberal voters, others fear it could alienate moderate voters and make the party less electable.

In summary, Sen. Bernie Sanders' introduction of the Medicare for All bill marks a significant shift in the U.S. health care debate, with support from key Democratic figures and the potential to shape the 2020 Democratic primary. However, the bill faces significant political and economic challenges, particularly in terms of financing and implementation.

David Oliver Relin, a journalist and adventurer, died on November 15, 2012, at the age of 49, after suffering from depression and taking his own life. His family stated that the controversy over the accuracy of his best-selling book, "Three Cups of Tea," co-authored with Greg Mortenson, significantly impacted his emotional and financial well-being. The book, which detailed Mortenson's efforts to build schools in Pakistan and Afghanistan, was later questioned by CBS News and Jon Krakauer, who published "Three Cups of Deceit." Mortenson acknowledged some inaccuracies, but the allegations damaged Relin's reputation and led to a federal lawsuit that was ultimately dismissed. Relin had previously established a career in humanitarian journalism, covering stories about child soldiers and his travels in Vietnam. Despite the controversy, he was passionate about inspiring young people and had begun work on a new book about doctors treating blindness in developing countries. His death highlights the personal toll that can come with the scrutiny of public figures and the media.

In a significant setback for ridesharing companies, Austin voters backed a measure requiring fingerprint background checks for drivers, effectively shutting down operations for Uber and Lyft in the city. The companies, which spent over $8 million to repeal the city ordinance, were outspent by their opponents by a ratio of 80-to-1. Despite their substantial financial backing, the measure passed with 56% of the vote, indicating a strong preference for stricter vetting processes among Austin residents.

Mayor Steve Adler has maintained a welcoming stance, offering to continue negotiations with the companies. However, the likelihood of a quick return is low, given the companies' history of playing hardball when faced with new regulations. Lyft has stated that this move is a "stand for a long-term path forward," while Uber expressed disappointment and indicated that it will suspend operations in Austin as of Monday. The withdrawal of Uber and Lyft is expected to create significant inconveniences for both customers and drivers, as Austin is a car-focused city with limited alternative transportation options. Additionally, drivers who relied on these services for income will now need to find other employment.

The outcome of the election is likely to encourage other cities to implement similar fingerprint background checks for ridesharing drivers. Austin's vote is the first major U.S. city to put such regulations to a public vote, and the results could set a precedent for other urban areas. Other cities, such as Atlanta and Houston, are also considering similar measures, with New York being one of the few major cities where Uber operates without requiring fingerprint background checks.

While the new regulations aim to reduce the risk of drivers committing crimes and ease the burden on emergency crews, the immediate impact on the local economy and transportation infrastructure is expected to be significant. The situation remains fluid, as the proposition is not yet final, and Austinites may still face unexpected changes in their transportation landscape.

Researchers at ETH Zurich University have developed a self-defense mechanism for ATMs inspired by the bombardier beetle, a creature known for its aggressive chemical defense system. The innovation involves creating a self-defending surface composed of sandwich-like layers of plastic, filled with two separate chemicals: hydrogen peroxide and manganese dioxide. When the surface is damaged, the chemicals mix, triggering a reaction that produces hot foam, water vapor, and oxygen. This foam, which is laden with dye, can mark both the banknotes and the thieves, making it difficult for criminals to escape detection. The foam also includes DNA nanoparticles for tracing the cash back to its source. This technology could be applied to various fields, such as agriculture and forestry, to protect valuable goods from vandalism. The design is a cost-effective alternative to the beetle's natural defense mechanism, which involves mixing hydrogen peroxide and hydroquinone in the abdomen. The researchers hope this technology will deter ATM thefts and make it harder for criminals to hide their activities.

Briggs Fussy and Brittney Fussy, who first met as children and served as ring bearer and flower girl at each other's godmother's wedding in 1995, have now rekindled their relationship and married each other 20 years later. The couple, now 22 years old, first crossed paths in high school in Minnesota, where Brittney sat in front of Briggs in government class. After some initial hesitation, Brittney discovered that the boy she knew from the wedding years ago was indeed her classmate. They began dating and eventually attended Mankato State University together.

Their unique story gained widespread attention when they walked down the aisle as bride and groom on January 10, 2020, with 310 family and friends in attendance. The couple's journey from childhood friends to coworkers and eventually to spouses has been a remarkable one, with their wedding day serving as a symbolic reunion of their past and present. "Everybody loves it -- especially my godmother, she takes all the credit," Briggs said, highlighting the positive reception their story has received.

The couple's story has not only brought them closer but has also garnered significant media attention, with articles and photographs documenting their journey. "We never expected having all this popularity, but we're enjoying it," Briggs added. The couple plans to keep the articles and photographs as mementos, promising to show them to their future children, ensuring that their unique story will be passed down through generations.

In an open letter to Dylan Farrow, actress Mira Sorvino has publicly apologized for her initial reluctance to support Farrow's claims of sexual abuse by her father, Woody Allen. Sorvino, who starred in Allen's 1995 film Mighty Aphrodite, acknowledges that she was initially swayed by the media's portrayal of the situation as a custody battle between Mia Farrow and Allen, and did not thoroughly investigate Farrow's claims. She expresses regret for not looking further into the situation and for not supporting Farrow when she wanted to believe the allegations were not true.

Sorvino states that her relationship with Allen on the set was friendly but not close, and she never personally experienced any inappropriate behavior. However, she recognizes that her failure to support Farrow is unacceptable. She was prompted to reconsider her stance after speaking with Ronan Farrow, Dylan's brother, about her own experiences with sexual harassment by Harvey Weinstein. Ronan directed her to additional information about the case, which made her reconsider her initial stance.

Sorvino's letter is part of a growing trend among actors who have worked with Allen, including Ellen Page and Greta Gerwig, who have also publicly distanced themselves from the filmmaker. Both Page and Gerwig have expressed regret for their involvement in Allen's films and the impact it had on Farrow's credibility. Sorvino emphasizes the importance of confronting and condemning such behavior, even when it involves individuals one admires or has benefited from in the past.

Sorvino's support for Farrow comes with a clear message: she will never work with Allen again. She believes that if one learns that a person may have committed such despicable acts, they must be exposed and condemned, and this exposure must have consequences. Her letter serves as a call to action, urging others to re-examine their own beliefs and actions in light of the ongoing revelations about sexual abuse in the entertainment industry.

This development highlights the complex and often painful process of re-evaluating one's relationships and past decisions in the face of new information and changing societal norms.

A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine found that firearm-related injuries and deaths temporarily decline by 20% during the National Rifle Association (NRA) annual conventions. The research, conducted by Dr. Anupam Jena of Harvard Medical School and Andrew Olenski of Columbia University, analyzed insurance claims from 2007 to 2015 and found a 63% reduction in firearm injuries in states hosting the NRA conventions. Nationally, the injury rate dropped by 20%. The study noted that the largest decreases were observed among men in southern and western states, where gun ownership is higher.

The NRA has criticized the findings, calling them "absurd" and questioning the statistical validity. However, the researchers suggest that the decrease in injuries is due to the reduced use of firearms by attendees and the temporary closure of shooting ranges and hunting grounds. They argue that even experienced gun owners are at risk of injury, and that gun safety remains a concern even among seasoned users.

The study's findings have broader implications for gun safety discussions. The researchers recommend investigating ways to make firearms safer, noting that other products have incorporated safety features, but firearms have not. This study adds to the ongoing debate on gun control and public safety, as membership in gun rights groups is reportedly increasing in response to recent high-profile shootings. Despite the NRA's growing membership, gun control advocates argue that the majority of Americans support stronger gun laws and safety measures.

On May 2, 2013, Carnell Moore, a 29-year-old from Beaumont, Texas, entered Terminal B at Houston's Bush Intercontinental Airport and fired two shots into the ceiling, causing panic among passengers. Hearing the gunfire, a Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agent confronted Moore, ordering him to drop his weapon. Moore turned towards the agent and was shot by the agent. Simultaneously, Moore turned his own gun on himself and fired, dying at the scene. Authorities found a black suitcase containing an AR15 assault weapon and additional ammunition in Moore's car. Moore had posted on social media earlier in the day that he intended to commit a mass shooting, and a suicide note was found on his body, expressing his struggle with a "monster inside" and his decision to spare others. The terminal was closed for several hours, and some passengers were rerouted to other terminals. The incident caused significant disruption to airport operations, with Terminal B being shut down for hours and incoming flights being rerouted.

Starbucks has recently updated its dress code policy, allowing employees to wear a wider range of clothing and hair colors. The new policy, effective immediately, permits employees to wear shirts in colors beyond solid black and white, including gray, navy, dark denim, and brown, as well as patterns. Dark wash jeans are now acceptable, and employees can also wear shorts, skirts, dresses, and pants. Perhaps most notably, Starbucks is now allowing employees to dye their hair any color, as long as the color is permanent or semi-permanent, to ensure food safety compliance.

The change in policy comes after years of complaints from employees about the restrictive hair color policy. A petition on Coworker.org, which garnered nearly 15,000 signatures, called for the change, stating that hair color can be an expression of one's true self. The new policy is part of a broader effort by Starbucks to create a more inclusive and individualized work environment, aligning with the company's mission to "inspire and nurture the human spirit."

While the new policy is more lenient, it still includes a "no list" of banned items, such as brightly colored shirts, hoodies, and UGG boots. The company has also introduced a new look book to guide employees on appropriate attire. The change has been well-received by employees, with many expressing excitement on social media. Some employees have already been wearing clothing that fits the new dress code guidelines, and the shift has been implemented in select stores, including the 47th & Broadway store in Manhattan and some Reserve stores.

Starbucks' executive vice president, Cosimo LaPorta, emphasized that the new dress code complements the passion that partners bring to their work. The company's president, Rossann Williams, noted that the policy change is part of a broader effort to offer the best partner experience and uplift the Starbucks brand. The new policy is seen as a step towards greater individual expression in the workplace, building on previous changes such as allowing visible tattoos and piercings.

Two men from Douglas, Georgia, Michael Mancil (30) and James Dryden Jr. (22), were arrested by Coffee County Sheriff's investigators on charges including selling methamphetamine, possession of marijuana, and possession of a weapon during the commission of a crime. The arrest came after a tip from a local gun shop alerted authorities that Mancil was attempting to purchase a large number of weapons. The investigation began when Mancil was under suspicion for drug sales.

The suspects were accused of planning to attack the High Frequency Active Auroral Research Facility (HAARP) in Alaska, a facility now owned by the University of Alaska Fairbanks. The HAARP facility has been the subject of numerous conspiracy theories, including claims that it manipulates the weather and controls minds. Mancil and Dryden allegedly believed that God instructed them to destroy the HAARP facility to release souls. The duo had amassed a significant arsenal, including four AR-15 rifles, four Glock handguns, a Remington rifle, and approximately 3,000 rounds of ammunition, which was seized during the raid.

The weapons were found at a residence on the 200 block of Jim Road in Coffee County, along with other items such as radios, two flak jackets, $5,500, and a small amount of marijuana. The Coffee County Sheriff, Doyle Wooten, expressed concern about the quantity of weapons collected by the suspects. Mancil's personality had reportedly changed in the past four to six weeks, leading to his arrest.

University of Alaska Fairbanks spokesperson Marmian Grimes stated that while the facility had faced threats before, this was the most significant threat they had encountered. She emphasized that HAARP is a scientific research facility studying the Earth's ionosphere and not a place for mind control or weather manipulation. The arrest of Mancil and Dryden has been seen as a relief by the university, as it helps to counteract the spread of conspiracy theories.

The case highlights the potential dangers of misinformation and conspiracy theories, as well as the importance of law enforcement in addressing such threats.

Steve Aisthorpe, a 55-year-old Scottish mountaineer and mission development worker for the Church of Scotland, has experienced closure after the remains of his two friends, Kristinn Rúnarsson and Þorsteinn Guðjónsson, were found in the Himalayas 30 years after they disappeared. The friends were last seen alive on October 18, 1988, at 21,650 feet on Pumori, a challenging peak near the Nepal-Tibet border. Their bodies were discovered by an American mountaineer and were brought to Kathmandu, Nepal, where a cremation service was held, and their ashes were returned to Iceland.

Aisthorpe, who had fallen ill and sent his friends to continue the expedition without him, recounted his distress during the search, describing the emptiness of their tent and the silence that followed. He initiated a helicopter search five days after the disappearance, which was unsuccessful. Over the years, Aisthorpe maintained contact with the families and friends of the missing climbers, eventually receiving news about the discovery of their remains three weeks ago.

The bodies were identified through photographs and personal items, including two camera films that have been sent to Australia for development. Aisthorpe plans to visit Iceland to meet the families and pay his respects. His faith played a significant role during the ordeal, providing comfort and guidance as he turned to God in prayer.

The tragedy did not discourage Aisthorpe from returning to Nepal and mountaineering. He spent several years working with the International Nepal Fellowship, a Christian charity involved in health and community development. The Church of Scotland, one of the founding partners of the United Mission to Nepal, has raised significant funds to rebuild communities affected by the 2015 earthquake, contributing to the construction of schools, water systems, and infrastructure.

Aisthorpe's story highlights the enduring impact of loss and the importance of faith and community in finding closure. The discovery of the remains of his friends has brought a sense of resolution and has united the community, allowing them to come together and honor the memory of the climbers.

At a recent tribute event for Alec Baldwin, former President Bill Clinton made a surprise appearance, delivering a speech that included several jabs at President Donald Trump. Clinton praised Baldwin's career, highlighting his genuine interest in helping others and his early forays into politics. He also noted that Baldwin had started making movies in his backyard at the age of five, and that his interest in politics began in elementary school. Clinton encouraged Baldwin to continue mocking Trump, stating, "You’ll probably win the next time. You need to think about running again." 

During the event, Robert De Niro also joined in on the criticism of Trump, praising Baldwin's impression and encouraging him to continue mocking the president. Other co-stars and family members, including Julianne Moore, Tracy Morgan, and Baldwin's children, also paid tribute to the actor. 

At the end of the show, Baldwin took the stage and made his own zingers, thanking his colleagues and family while also poking fun at them. Baldwin confirmed that he would return to "Saturday Night Live" to play Donald Trump this fall, despite his busy schedule, stating, "Yea, we're going to fit that in. I think people have enjoyed it." He noted that the number of Trump impersonations would be limited, with only "a couple celery sticks" rather than a "whole meal" of blonde wigs and orange bronzer. Baldwin, who has hosted "SNL" a record 17 times, has made his Trump impersonation one of his most memorable sketches.

The family of Walter Scott, an African-American man fatally shot by a white police officer in North Charleston, South Carolina, has reached a $6.5 million settlement with the city. The settlement was approved by the North Charleston City Council, marking the largest such payout in recent high-profile killings of black men by police. The shooting, captured on video by a passerby, showed the officer, Michael Slager, shooting Scott in the back while he was running away. Slager was fired and jailed, and was indicted for murder in June. The city chose to settle rather than face a civil lawsuit, aiming to avoid further public unrest and to focus on the criminal trial. The settlement includes provisions to protect city employees from being sued and will be split between the family and donated to the Red Cross for flood victims. North Charleston officials emphasized the peaceful response to the incident and the city's swift actions as key factors in reaching the settlement. The case has sparked broader discussions on police reform and the use of force against black men. The settlement is seen as a precedent for handling similar cases, emphasizing the importance of dialogue and peaceful resolution.

A lawsuit has been filed in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court by Robert and Krystsina Trostle against Kennywood Entertainment, alleging negligence and seeking damages in excess of $35,000. The Trostles claim that Robert contracted a harmful parasite, microsporidia, after being splashed with water during a ride on the Raging Rapids water ride at Kennywood Park on July 2, 2023. The lawsuit states that the water surrounding the ride was "dirty, stagnant, and sludge-like," and the waterfall was not operating, raising concerns about the cleanliness and safety of the water.

Robert Trostle's left eye became inflamed, itchy, red, photosensitive, and severely painful over the next two days. He was diagnosed with acute conjunctivitis on July 5 and given antibiotics, but his condition worsened. On July 14, he was diagnosed with microsporidia keratitis, which required an extremely painful surgical procedure to scrape the parasite from his eye. The lawsuit alleges that Kennywood did not have adequate policies and procedures to inspect the water used on the ride to eliminate or reduce the dangers posed by microsporidia and ensure its safety.

Kennywood Entertainment's spokesman, Nick Paradise, stated that the company's safety is a top priority and that the parasite claim is an allegation that has not been proven. The Allegheny County Health Department took samples from the ride's water after the incident but has not released the results, despite a Right To Know request from the Trostles' attorney. The health department is still investigating the matter.

This case is reminiscent of another incident in June 2016, where a 18-year-old, Lauren Seitz, contracted a brain-eating amoeba, Naegleria fowleri, after rafting at the U.S. National Whitewater Center in North Carolina. The park's water quality was found to be inadequate, leading to the park's closure for nearly two months and changes in its filtration and disinfection systems. The Trostles' case highlights the ongoing challenges in ensuring the safety of water rides and the potential for rare but severe health outcomes.

Wind shear significantly impacts hurricane formation and intensity, particularly in the vertical direction from the surface to the top of the troposphere. Key factors include the difference in wind speed and direction between the surface and upper levels, typically measured over a 700-mile diameter area. Wind shear can disrupt the heat engine function of tropical cyclones by removing necessary heat and moisture, and can distort the storm's structure, making it less efficient. Dr. Bill Gray highlighted the importance of zonal wind shear, especially in the Atlantic and central Pacific, where large vertical shear inhibits tropical storm development.

Hurricanes require specific conditions to intensify, with a general rule of thumb that shear must be 20 knots or less for intensification. However, powerful hurricanes like Hurricane Wilma can withstand shear values as high as 40 knots. The University of Wisconsin CIMSS site provides real-time wind shear analyses, crucial for monitoring developing storms.

Recent developments with Hurricane Irma illustrate the unpredictability of hurricane tracks and intensities. Irma, a Cape Verde hurricane, rapidly intensified to a Category 3 hurricane in just a day, with the potential to become a Category 4. Its path remains uncertain, with models predicting various outcomes, from a direct hit on the U.S. to a harmlessly offshore encounter. The ongoing threat of Irma underscores the need for preparedness, especially in regions still recovering from Hurricane Harvey.

The 2017 Atlantic hurricane season, already above average, highlights the persistent risk of severe storms. Factors such as neutral ENSO conditions, warmer sea surface temperatures, and the strength of the West African monsoon contribute to the increased likelihood of an active season. Coastal areas, particularly the Gulf of Mexico and Atlantic Ocean, remain at risk throughout the season, with the peak activity period from September 10 to November 30.

The incident involving the shooting of a European bison in Germany has sparked controversy over wildlife management practices. The bison, a species not seen in the wild in Germany for over 250 years, was shot by local hunters at the instruction of the head of a public order office in Brandenburg. This action, despite the bison being a "strongly protected animal" in Germany, has been criticized by environmental groups, particularly the World Wildlife Fund (WWF), who argue that such a decision reflects a lack of professional training in wildlife management.

The European bison, Europe’s largest land mammal, is considered vulnerable and is protected by international conservation bodies. The bison, likely a bull, had been roaming the border between Germany and Poland before entering the Bundesrepublik. Brandenburg's Environment Minister, Jörg Vogelsänger, stated that bison are not considered dangerous, and suggested that tranquilizer darts could have been used instead of lethal force.

The incident highlights the challenges of managing wildlife in areas where such species have been absent for centuries. The European bison, once on the brink of extinction, has made a remarkable comeback in Poland, where it is now a national symbol and a key part of the Bialowieza Forest, a UNESCO World Heritage site. This forest, which spans both Poland and Belarus, is home to a diverse range of wildlife, including wolves, lynx, and bears.

However, the reintroduction of bison and other large herbivores has brought new challenges. The bison's low genetic diversity, resulting from a small number of ancestors, poses a risk to the species' long-term survival. To address this, efforts are underway to expand the bison's range and manage their populations through controlled culling, which has been controversial among conservationists.

The case of the bison shooting in Germany also raises broader questions about the management of wildlife in Europe. In Poland, for example, there is a debate over the balance between conservation and traditional forestry practices. Some argue that allowing nature to manage itself, as seen in the exclusion zone around the Chernobyl nuclear disaster, could be more beneficial than human intervention. Others advocate for more open, wild grassland areas to support large herbivores.

In conclusion, the shooting of the bison in Germany underscores the complex challenges of wildlife management in Europe, particularly in reintroducing species that have been absent for centuries. It highlights the need for better training and more innovative approaches to ensure the long-term survival of these species while balancing human interests and ecological needs.

Facebook and Microsoft have entered into a complex patent deal that involves Microsoft acquiring 925 patents from AOL and then selling 650 of those patents to Facebook for $550 million. This move is seen as a strategic countermeasure against Google’s dominance in the tech industry, as both companies are increasingly aligned in their efforts to challenge Google’s market position. The deal is particularly significant for Facebook, which is preparing for its initial public offering (IPO) and is keen on building a robust intellectual property portfolio to protect its interests.

The agreement not only bolsters Facebook’s patent arsenal but also provides it with a stronger position in its ongoing patent dispute with Yahoo. Yahoo had sued Facebook for patent infringement, and this deal could potentially give Facebook additional leverage in its legal battles. Additionally, the partnership between Microsoft and Facebook underscores their mutual interest in countering Google’s influence, especially in the realm of search and social networking.

Microsoft’s decision to sell a portion of the AOL patents to Facebook is part of a broader strategy to streamline its own patent portfolio. By retaining some of the patents, Microsoft can still leverage them for its own benefit, while allowing Facebook to acquire the ones that are most relevant to its business. This arrangement is seen as a strategic move to maintain a balance of power in the tech industry, with both companies aiming to weaken Google’s competitive edge.

The deal also highlights the growing importance of patent acquisition in the tech industry, as companies increasingly recognize the value of owning a strong portfolio of intellectual property. For Facebook, this move is crucial as it prepares to go public and faces increasing legal challenges from other tech giants. The partnership between Microsoft and Facebook, while ostensibly against Google, also serves to strengthen their own positions in the market, creating a more competitive and dynamic tech landscape.

The document discusses the controversy surrounding the shutdown of PonyArchive.org, a website offering free episodes of the animated series "My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic," and the ensuing conflict with Hasbro. Bronies, adult male fans of the show, rallied around the site, with one posting a defiant message to Hasbro. The incident sparked a debate within the brony community about whether the site's response was justified or immature. The show, originally targeted at children, gained a significant adult following, drawing praise for its quality and appeal to a broader audience. The controversy highlights the tension between corporate copyright enforcement and fan communities, as well as the unique dynamics of online subcultures.

In a rare case of theft, an employee of the Royal Canadian Mint in Ottawa, Leston Lawrence, was found guilty of stealing 22 gold "pucks" from his workplace. His job involved taking small samples from batches of molten gold for purity testing, often working alone and out of sight of the only security camera. Lawrence managed to sell 17 of the pucks for approximately $130,000, but was ultimately caught when a bank employee alerted authorities to suspicious cheques. Lawrence was sentenced to 30 months in jail and fined $190,000, the estimated value of the missing gold. He used the proceeds to purchase a house in Jamaica and a boat in Florida.

The evidence against Lawrence was circumstantial, as no one witnessed the theft, and there was no video evidence. However, the pucks matched the unique ladle used at the mint, and Vaseline and latex gloves were found in his locker. Four unsold pucks were also recovered from a safety deposit box. The judge noted that Lawrence set off the metal detector more often than any other employee, but subsequent wand checks did not trigger alarms.

The sentencing took into account the Crown's request for a three-year prison term and the defense's argument for an 18-month sentence. The defense also argued that Lawrence should only have to pay back $130,000, the amount he made from selling the pucks, rather than the estimated $190,000 value. The judge's decision was seen as meticulous and careful by the defense lawyer.
