For $1, buyers can offset one chicken-sandwich meal, with 80% of proceeds going to It Gets Better and the Williams Institute. Frank emphasizes that buying offsets provides more funding for gay-rights causes than boycotting Chick-fil-A. The site has generated interest but has yet to see significant sales. Frank also runs the non-profit Center for Class Action Fairness LLC, which supports consumers in class action lawsuits. The launch of ChickenOffset.com came amid ongoing protests against Chick-fil-A's opposition to same-sex marriage, highlighting the tension between supporting a business and aligning with its social stances.

On October 27, 2017, Catalonia's regional parliament voted to establish an independent Catalan Republic, a move that sparked a political crisis in Spain. The vote, which passed with 70 in favor and 10 against, was met with celebrations outside the parliament in Barcelona. However, the Spanish government, led by Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy, opposed the move and sought to halt it. Rajoy urged the Spanish Senate to approve constitutional measures that would allow the central government to take control of Catalonia's autonomous powers and dismiss regional President Carles Puigdemont and his cabinet. 

The Spanish government's proposed measures, including the potential sacking of Catalan leaders and curtailment of the parliament's powers, were aimed at restoring legality and order. Rajoy emphasized that the measures were necessary to protect the rights of all Catalans. The Spanish government's actions were met with criticism, with some arguing that they would only exacerbate the conflict. 

Meanwhile, thousands of supporters gathered outside the parliament to celebrate the vote, while opposition lawmakers boycotted the session in protest. The move to declare independence was opposed by all opposition parties in Catalonia and by the Spanish government. The Spanish Senate was expected to approve the government's measures, which would allow the central government to take direct control of Catalonia. 

The declaration of independence was seen as a significant challenge to Spain's unity, with Catalonia representing a fifth of Spain's GDP and its people divided on the issue of independence. The situation remained tense, with the Spanish government promising to call a new regional election once order was restored. The crisis highlighted the deep divisions within Spain and the potential for further conflict if a resolution was not found.

Two New Mexico State University students, McKinnah Sinclair, 18, and Charlie Daniels, 19, who were reported missing earlier this week, have been located in Nampa, Idaho, by the Las Cruces Police Department. The students were found in a red Ford Focus, which belongs to Daniels' parents, though the license plate was fake. The vehicle had been reported stolen, but the Nampa Police Department did not pursue charges due to the nature of the relationship between the students and the parents. The students were observed by a Nampa police officer who noted the car was traveling well below the speed limit, leading to a traffic stop. Sinclair and Daniels were the only occupants of the vehicle. 

The students had switched the license plates before embarking on their journey, traveling from El Paso, Texas, to California and then to Idaho. They were captured on surveillance footage at an ATM in Beverly Hills, California, indicating they had traveled on their own and had not informed their families of their plans. Sinclair is a member of the NMSU cheerleading squad and is majoring in pre-social work, while Daniels is studying kinesiology. Their families have made arrangements to have them returned to New Mexico.

The Las Cruces Police Department received assistance from various law enforcement agencies across multiple states, including New Mexico, Texas, Arizona, California, Nevada, and Idaho. The students were last seen at a Rare El Paso hip-hop concert on February 3, and missing person affidavits were filed with the Las Cruces Police Department on Tuesday morning. The exact reason for their disappearance and their final destination remain unclear.

A Brazilian couple, Adriana and Leandro, who had been searching for their birth mothers for most of their lives, discovered they were unknowingly married to each other and had a child together. Adriana, 39, and Leandro, 37, had been together for seven years and had a six-year-old daughter. Both were abandoned as infants by their mothers, who were named Maria, and had been searching for them for years. 

Adriana, a cosmetics saleswoman, contacted a radio station in her hometown to help her find her mother, while Leandro, a truck driver, had learned of his mother's abandonment when he was eight years old. They met for the first time ten years ago and fell in love, moving in together. 

During an interview on Radio Globo's 'The Time Is Now' program, which specializes in reuniting lost relatives, Adriana learned that her mother had also given birth to a son, Leandro, whom she had never met. Upon hearing this, Adriana broke down, sobbing uncontrollably and expressing fear that Leandro might not want her anymore. 

Despite the shocking revelation, the couple vowed to stay together, stating that their love had developed independently of their familial relationship. They claimed that only death would separate them, and that they believed this was God's will. Adriana and Leandro had never legally married, and their union was technically void under Brazilian law. However, they expressed their commitment to each other and their plans for the future.

The Women of NASA LEGO set, created by Maia Weinstock, deputy editor of MIT News, is set to launch as an official LEGO product, celebrating the contributions of five pioneering women to the U.S. space program. The set honors Margaret Hamilton, a computer scientist who led the development of software for the Apollo missions; Mae Jemison, the first African-American woman in space; Katherine Johnson, a key figure in the Mercury and Apollo programs; Sally Ride, the first American woman in space; and Nancy Grace Roman, a key figure in the planning of the Hubble Space Telescope. Weinstock's inspiration stems from her love for space and her desire to promote female representation in STEM fields. Since 2009, she has created LEGO figurines for notable scientists and engineers, including MIT faculty members and Jane Goodall, aiming to boost the visibility of female scientists. The set, which includes a diverse group of women in terms of their fields, cultural backgrounds, and ages, is expected to encourage more young girls to pursue STEM careers. Weinstock hopes the set will contribute to improving the perception of women in STEM fields and inspire future generations to engage in scientific endeavors.

Bana Alabed, a seven-year-old girl from Aleppo, has written an open letter to President Donald Trump, appealing for his intervention to bring peace to Syria. The letter, shared by Bana's mother, Fatemah, highlights Bana's personal experiences of the war and her hope for a better future. Bana escaped Aleppo with her family in December 2016 during mass evacuations and is now living in Turkey, where she has been able to enjoy peace and attend school. However, she notes that millions of Syrian children are still suffering, emphasizing that they deserve peace and protection.

Bana's Twitter account, which gained worldwide attention for its messages from besieged East Aleppo, has now turned to calls for an end to the fighting. The letter reflects Bana's desire to befriend the new US president, urging him to take action to save Syrian children, stating, "You must do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace like you."

The US president's position on Syria is not yet clear. During his campaign, Trump expressed admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who supports Syria's President Assad. However, the Pentagon has denied conducting joint combat missions with Russia, while the White House has indicated openness to cooperation. Russia, Iran, and Turkey have recently pledged to enforce a three-week ceasefire in Syria, but the agreement's sustainability remains uncertain.

The Syrian conflict has claimed over 300,000 lives, including at least 15,000 children, with thousands more displaced. Bana's letter underscores the personal impact of the war on children and the urgent need for international intervention to bring about peace.

The document discusses a significant increase in Legionnaires' disease cases in Genesee County, Michigan, following the city of Flint switching its water source to the Flint River. The Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) reported 87 cases from June 2014 to November 2015, with 10 fatalities. This is a substantial increase from the previous years, which saw between 6 and 13 cases annually. While the MDHHS cannot conclusively link the increase to the Flint water crisis, it is treating the situation with the same urgency as the lead contamination issue in Flint.

Health officials are conducting investigations, including evaluating clinical and environmental samples, to determine the source of the bacteria. The MDHHS has been working with the Michigan Department of Environmental Quality (DEQ), the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to address the issue. They have also been informing hospitals in Genesee County about the increase in cases and recommending actions to prevent future incidents.

Legionnaires' disease is a respiratory illness caused by the bacteria Legionella, which thrives in warm water. It is not spread from person to person but can be contracted by inhaling contaminated water droplets. The disease primarily affects individuals with weakened immune systems, such as the elderly, smokers, and those with chronic lung conditions.

The Flint water crisis, which began in 2014 when the city switched its water source to the Flint River, has been a significant public health concern. The river water was not properly treated, leading to increased lead levels in the water supply, which caused widespread health issues, including lead poisoning in children. The Flint River water also lacked proper corrosion control, leading to the proliferation of Legionella bacteria in the water system.

The MDHHS has been releasing reports and conducting surveillance to ensure appropriate actions are taken to protect residents. They have also been working with local health departments and the clinical community to enhance surveillance and testing for Legionnaires' disease. The state is taking the issue seriously, acknowledging the increase in cases as part of the ongoing Flint water crisis.

In response to the increased Legionnaires' cases, the MDHHS has not changed its recommendations for residents regarding the use of bottled water and water filters. The state is also considering the possibility that the increase in cases might be related to the water supply, although definitive proof is still pending.

The Flint water crisis has been a complex and multifaceted issue, involving multiple levels of government and various stakeholders. While the MDHHS is taking steps to address the increase in Legionnaires' cases, the broader issue of water quality and public health remains a critical concern for the residents of Flint and the state of Michigan.

In the wake of a rapidly spreading wildfire in Southern California, residents in the path of the blaze faced urgent evacuation orders. The fire, which broke out on Monday, quickly grew to more than 15 square miles, consuming decades-old vegetation. The intense winds, gusting over 60 mph, exacerbated the situation, pushing the flames towards Santa Paula, a city of 30,000 people, and the nearby city of Ventura, with a population of 106,000. Thousands of homes were evacuated, with the majority of evacuations occurring in Santa Paula. The fire's rapid growth was described as "exponential" by Chief Mark Lorenzen of the Ventura County Fire Department, emphasizing the critical need for firefighters to focus on evacuating people and protecting structures.

One resident, Moore, who had moved to Coronado Circle about eight years ago, was unprepared for the fire's proximity to her home. The neighborhood, which opens onto hundreds of acres of dry brush, posed a known risk of fire, but Moore's experience of witnessing the fire approach so closely was still a shock. The evacuation of Thomas Aquinas College, a school with about 350 students, further highlighted the widespread impact of the disaster. One person was reported killed in an accident related to the evacuation, and at least two structures had been destroyed.

The National Weather Service continued to warn of strong winds, which forced the grounding of firefighting aircraft late on Monday night. Despite these challenges, firefighters and aircraft from neighboring counties were mobilizing to assist in the effort. The situation remained volatile, with thousands of homes in the area experiencing power outages. The relentless winds and the fire's rapid spread underscored the urgent and complex nature of the emergency response required.

The Honolulu City Council has passed a bill that bans pedestrians from looking at mobile devices while crossing streets or highways, including crosswalks, with the aim of enhancing safety. The bill, which passed with a 7-2 vote, does not apply to talking on the phone and allows the use of audio equipment. Pedestrians caught violating the rule could face fines ranging from $15 to $99 for a first offense, with higher penalties for repeat offenders. The measure, which is currently awaiting Mayor Kirk Caldwell's approval, would come into effect 90 days after signing. While supporters argue that the bill will hold pedestrians accountable for their actions on the road, critics view it as intrusive and an example of local government overreach. The bill's author claims to have been inspired by high school students, while opponents suggest that the city council should focus on more pressing issues. Honolulu Police Department has expressed support for the measure, and if signed, enforcement could begin in October.

The document discusses the efforts of the Internet Archive to preserve web pages and their references, aiming to fix broken links on the web. This initiative involves archiving pages and the pages they reference, ensuring that when referenced pages change or disappear, a link to the version that was live when the original page was written is still available. The goal is to maintain the integrity of web content and provide a historical record of the internet.

Additionally, the document includes a job posting for a live-in caretaker position at God's Little People Cat Rescue on the Greek island of Syros. The job offers free housing and a salary, with the opportunity to live on a "small paradise" and interact with cats. The posting is genuine and intended to attract potential candidates.

Lastly, the document provides information about RESQCATS, a non-profit cat sanctuary in Santa Barbara, California. RESQCATS focuses on rescuing, caring for, and adopting abandoned cats and kittens. The sanctuary emphasizes the importance of personal interaction with each cat to find the best home, considering factors such as the cat's personality, behavior, and compatibility with potential adopters. RESQCATS also offers support to those who have lost their cats and are considering adopting a new one. The sanctuary's president, Jeffyne Telson, encourages people to contact her for more information or to adopt a cat.

Honda has released a Super Bowl commercial that pays homage to the 1986 film "Ferris Bueller's Day Off," starring Matthew Broderick. The ad, produced by RPA, shows Broderick as Ferris calling in sick from a film shoot and enjoying a day off in his new 2012 CR-V. This extended version, revealed by Jalopnik, is a great tribute to the original, with Broderick seamlessly re-creating his character. The commercial includes over 20 references to the movie, ranging from obvious to subtle, encouraging fans to find them. This campaign celebrates the launch of the all-new CR-V and is a significant crowd-pleaser, satisfying those who had hoped for a sequel while honoring the original film.

A video of Chinese bank employees being publicly spanked during a training session has sparked outrage and led to the suspension of two executives. The incident occurred at the Rural Commercial Bank in Shanxi province, where an unnamed trainer from the Shanghai Hongfeng Leadership Academy reportedly used a wooden stick to spank eight employees, including four women, for poor performance. The punishment was carried out in front of around 200 colleagues, and the video, recorded by an audience member, quickly went viral, drawing widespread criticism for the brutal treatment.

According to the Shanxi Rural Credit Cooperatives Union, the training session was part of a "Breakthrough in Performance" program, where employees were graded and punished. The bank has since suspended several managing personnel and asked the Leadership Academy and its trainer to apologize publicly. The trainer, Jiang Yang, acknowledged that his methods might not be universally accepted but defended physical punishment as an effective way to raise consciousness.

The video also showed that 16 employees were forced to have their heads shaved as another form of punishment. Jiang Yang later apologized and explained that the aim of the training was to improve employees' thinking and encourage competitiveness. The Shanxi Rural Credit Cooperatives Union confirmed the incident and stated that the two executives, including the bank's president, were suspended for failing to properly assess the training. The bank is also considering compensation for the spanked employees.

This incident highlights the controversial and often extreme methods used in some corporate training programs in China, which have drawn significant criticism for violating employee rights. The public reaction and subsequent suspension of the executives underscore the growing awareness and sensitivity towards such practices in Chinese society.

Jon Stewart's "Rally to Restore Sanity" on the National Mall has sparked mixed reactions, with some fans concerned about Stewart's credibility and others hoping to leverage his influence for political gain. Stewart, known for his comedic role on "The Daily Show," is positioning himself as a cultural figure with significant sway, much like Johnny Carson. His rally, co-hosted with Stephen Colbert, aims to address political divisions and promote voter turnout, particularly among young and disenchanted Democrats.

Stewart's recent interview with President Obama on his show highlighted his ability to balance humor and critique. Stewart's questions, which echoed liberal concerns about Obama's cautious approach, were met with a mix of humor and serious responses from the president. Obama defended his policies and administration, emphasizing the progress made despite challenges. The interview was part of a broader strategy by Obama to reach younger voters through unconventional media platforms.

Stewart's political engagement carries both risks and opportunities. While some fear he might lose his outsider credibility by participating in mainstream politics, others view it as a strategic move to maintain his relevance and influence. Stewart's rally is seen as a publicity stunt to promote his shows and harness the voices of disaffected moderates. However, there are concerns that Stewart might alienate his core audience, which is less polarized than the viewers of traditional cable news.

The event's success will depend on Stewart's ability to navigate these risks while maintaining his comedic and critical edge. By framing the rally as a response to political divisions and a call for unity, Stewart aims to bridge gaps and encourage civic engagement. The rally's outcome will be closely watched, as it could set a precedent for future political interventions by media personalities.

RAF Typhoon fighter jets have been scrambled twice this month in response to potential terror threats in UK airspace, raising the possibility of a decision to shoot down a civilian airliner. On March 22, a conversation on an United Airlines flight included "ransom" and "hostage," leading to the interception of a Delta Airlines plane. Two Typhoons were launched from RAF Coningsby in just minutes. On March 2, an American Airlines flight reported a passenger attempting to enter the cockpit, prompting Typhoons and Tornados to intercept. Both incidents turned out to be false alarms. These alerts, part of counter-terrorism measures introduced after 9/11, are triggered about once a month out of the three million flights that pass through UK airspace annually. The procedures involve informing the prime minister or designated ministers, who could order the destruction of a civilian airliner if necessary. RAF jets also intercepted Russian bombers recently, highlighting ongoing tensions. The UK's Strategic Defence Review after the general election will likely lead to cuts, with the RAF, Royal Navy, and Army competing for funding.

Thirty years after the brutal murder of 14-year-old Claire Hough on Torrey Pines State Beach in 1984, San Diego homicide investigators have identified two suspects through DNA evidence collected at the scene. Hough was found beaten, strangled, stabbed, and with one of her breasts severed. She was staying with her grandparents at the time of her death. In November 2012, detectives used DNA analysis to link Kevin Charles Brown, a former San Diego Police Department criminalist, and Ronald Clyde Tatro to the crime. Brown, who worked as a criminalist from 1982 to 2002, was found dead in Cuyamaca State Park in October 2014, with his death ruled as a suicide. Tatro, identified as a suspect in August 2014, died in a boating accident in 2011. The investigation revealed that Brown had no connection to the evidence or the murder investigation, while Tatro's death prevented any further action. The case remains unsolved, with authorities encouraging anyone with information to come forward. The murder of Hough is part of a series of similar killings, including the 1978 murder of 15-year-old Barbara Nantais, also found on the same beach, which shares some similarities but was not directly linked to Hough's case.

Lamar Austin, a 30-year-old military veteran and father of four, was fired from his job as a part-time security guard for missing work to be with his wife, Lindsay, at the birth of their newborn son, Cainan, on New Year's Day. Despite being an "at-will" employee, Austin's termination drew significant public attention and support. Local unions and business managers offered Austin job opportunities in the electrical field, providing him with potential career advancement and financial stability. Additionally, a GoFundMe campaign raised over $1,000 in a single day to support the Austin family.

Austin's story highlighted the challenges faced by part-time and temporary workers in New Hampshire, where there are few legal protections for employees who need to take time off for family reasons. State Senator Dan Feltes and other lawmakers have proposed legislation to offer flexible working arrangements, but the current lack of such protections has left many workers in precarious situations. The incident also sparked discussions about the need for better family leave policies in New Hampshire, especially for part-time and temporary workers.

Austin expressed gratitude for the support he received and hopes that his experience will contribute to broader policy changes. He is now considering a career in the electrical field, which could offer him more stability and a higher income. The public's response to Austin's story underscores the growing demand for better work-life balance and family-friendly policies in the workplace.

EgyptAir Flight MS804, an Airbus A320 carrying 66 passengers and crew, disappeared over the Mediterranean Sea while en route from Paris to Cairo. The flight lost contact with air traffic controllers shortly after entering Egyptian airspace. Early reports suggested the plane may have crashed, but EgyptAir later clarified that debris found in the Mediterranean was not from the plane. The search for the missing aircraft continues, involving Egyptian, French, and Greek authorities. Egyptian officials believe a terrorist attack is more likely than a technical failure, though no definitive cause has been determined. The incident has raised concerns about Egypt's aviation safety record, with previous incidents including a hijacking and a terrorist attack on a Russian airliner. The U.S. and other nations have offered assistance in the search and investigation.

On Tuesday, October 30, 2018, a tragic accident occurred north of Rochester, Indiana, resulting in the deaths of three children and critically injuring a fourth. The incident unfolded around 7 a.m., just before sunrise, when a 9-year-old girl and her twin 6-year-old brothers, Xzavier and Mason Ingle, and their 9-year-old sister, Alivia Stahl, were struck by a northbound pickup truck as they crossed SR 25 to board a school bus. The siblings were students at Mentone Elementary School and residents of a nearby rural mobile home community. The pickup truck, driven by 24-year-old Alyssa Shepherd of Rochester, struck the children as they crossed the southbound lane, killing them at the scene. The injured 11-year-old boy, Maverik Lowe, suffered multiple broken bones and was airlifted to a Fort Wayne hospital, where he underwent surgery.

The Indiana State Police, led by Sgt. Tony Slocum, were on the scene and are interviewing witnesses and conducting a crash reconstruction. The driver, Alyssa Shepherd, was arrested and charged with three counts of reckless homicide and one misdemeanor count of passing a school bus with an extended stop-arm, causing bodily injury. The incident has deeply affected the community, with Governor Eric Holcomb and his wife, Janet, expressing their condolences and urging prayers for the families.

The Tippecanoe Valley School Corp. responded by dispatching counselors to its schools to support students, staff, and parents. The tragedy underscores the importance of adhering to traffic laws, particularly when school buses are in operation, and highlights the shared responsibility of road users to ensure the safety of children. The community is coming together to mourn the loss of these young lives and to offer support to the families during this difficult time.

The National Museum of Fine Arts in Havana, Cuba, has reported the theft of 70 artworks, mostly from the "Turn of the Century" period, with a total estimated value of over $1.5 million. UNESCO condemned the theft, warning of the risk of illicit trafficking of cultural assets. The artworks, including paintings by Cuban artist Leopoldo Romañach, were discovered after several pieces were put on sale in Miami, home to a significant Cuban exile community. Cuban authorities confirmed the robbery but did not disclose the exact number of stolen pieces. The theft involved cutting the canvases and carefully repositioning the frames, making it difficult to detect. The Cuban Minister of Culture, Rafael Bernal, was dismissed following the theft, though no official reason was given. Law enforcement officials in both Cuba and the United States are investigating the case. A Miami art dealer, Ramon Cernuda, first reported the theft after purchasing a painting that was later confirmed to be missing from the museum. Cernuda noted that the theft is unusual in Cuba, where museums are typically well-guarded. Despite the complexity of the theft, Cernuda expects the stolen artworks to be returned to Cuba.

A concerning incident involving a list of alleged campus rapists has been reported multiple times across Columbia University's campus. The list, written in silver marker, has appeared in women's bathroom stalls in Hamilton, Lerner, and Butler halls. The names on the list are the same across all versions, suggesting a single author or a coordinated effort. Campus media, including Bwog and The Lion, have been tipped about the lists and have posted updates on their presence and removal.

Public Safety has taken steps to address the issue, closing down bathrooms and removing the graffiti. However, the lists have been quickly reappeared, indicating a persistent and possibly coordinated effort to spread the information. The incident has sparked debate about the appropriate methods for addressing sexual assault on campus, with some arguing that vigilante justice is not the best approach.

The case is reminiscent of a similar incident that occurred at Brown University in 1990, where lists of alleged rapists were also found in bathrooms. At Columbia, the administration has stated that the lists will be treated as graffiti, which could result in disciplinary and legal consequences for the author. Campus media outlets have been cautious about publishing the names, citing concerns about privacy and the potential for a witch hunt.

The incident highlights the ongoing challenges of addressing sexual assault on college campuses and the complex balance between supporting victims and ensuring fair and legal processes. The community is urged to report any further sightings of the lists to campus authorities.

A new study presented at the 108th Annual Meeting of the American Sociological Association reveals that people exhibit more empathy towards abused puppies and full-grown dogs than towards adult human victims of abuse, but this empathy is similar for both children and puppies. Jack Levin, the Irving and Betty Brudnick Professor of Sociology and Criminology at Northeastern University, and Arnold Arluke, a sociology professor at the same institution, conducted the study. They surveyed 240 college students, primarily white and aged 18-25, who read one of four fictional news articles about a brutal beating, with the only difference being the identity of the victim: a one-year-old child, an adult in his thirties, a puppy, or a 6-year-old dog. Participants rated their empathy levels for each victim. The results showed higher empathy for the abused child, puppy, and dog compared to the abused adult. This finding suggests that adult humans are perceived as capable of self-protection, while full-grown dogs are seen as dependent and vulnerable, much like puppies and children.

Levin noted that the age of the victim is more significant in eliciting empathy than the species, with adult humans receiving less empathy than younger victims. The researchers also found that women were more empathetic towards both human and animal victims, possibly due to biological factors linked to childbirth and childrearing. However, the study's sample was limited to college students, so it is unclear if these findings apply to a broader age range. The study implies that dogs and cats, as family pets, are often attributed human-like characteristics, which could influence empathy levels.

North Korean authorities have arrested several hundred relatives of Jang Song-thaek, the recently executed uncle of Supreme Leader Kim Jong-un. The arrests reportedly took place on December 13, the day after Jang's execution, and were carried out by the Ministry of State Security. The scale of the arrests underscores the extent to which Kim Jong-un is purging his uncle's influence from the country's history. Jang was accused of 24 crimes, including undermining the party and creating illusions about himself. His relatives, including distant family members, were taken away, and even those outside Pyongyang are not safe. The Daily NK, a newspaper run by defectors, reported that those arrested may face execution or life in labor colonies.

The execution of Jang Song-thaek was part of a broader struggle for power within North Korea. According to South Korean and American officials, Jang's forces were defeated in a battle for control of lucrative fishing grounds, which Jang had seized from the military. This defeat, along with Jang's business and political activities, led to his downfall. The execution was carried out using antiaircraft machine guns, a method similar to that used against some North Korean artists. Jang's execution and the subsequent arrests of his relatives were seen as a way to consolidate Kim Jong-un's control over the military and the country's limited sources of foreign currency.

Dennis Rodman, the flamboyant former NBA star, recently visited North Korea for the third time. His latest trip was sponsored by the online betting company Paddy Power, which later withdrew its connection due to the global scrutiny and condemnation of North Korea's human rights record. Rodman praised the local basketball players he trained and stated he would return in another week. His visits to North Korea, despite international criticism, have been described as "basketball diplomacy" aimed at improving relations and promoting sports.

The arrests of Jang Song-thaek's relatives and the execution itself highlight the severe consequences faced by those associated with the deposed leader. The actions taken by North Korean authorities indicate a desire to erase Jang's influence and maintain strict control over the country's elite.

Starting November 3, new security measures will be implemented on Chicago Transit Authority (CTA) trains as part of a federal counter-terrorism initiative. Passengers will be randomly selected to have their bags, purses, or suitcases swabbed for explosive compounds by Chicago police officers using mobile screening equipment. The process, which takes about 30 seconds, aims to enhance safety without significantly impacting commuters' travel times. Commander Nancy Lipman emphasized the importance of passenger cooperation, stating that the 20 to 30 seconds of delay is "probably priceless" in terms of safety. However, skepticism from both riders and a public transit expert has been expressed. The measure is being funded with a portion of a $3.5 million federal anti-terrorism grant. Police will set up screening tables at randomly selected stations during rush hours, with four to five officers per table. While the screenings are voluntary, those who refuse will be ordered to leave the station and face potential arrest. Critics argue that the screenings may be ineffective, as riders can opt out and avoid detection. The CTA expects the screenings to have minimal impact on commutes, with more than 229 million rail rides taken in 2013 across its 140 stations.

Actress Jamie Denbo, known for her role in Orange Is the New Black, recently spoke out against ageism in Hollywood on Twitter. Denbo was told she was "too old" to play the wife of a 57-year-old actor, despite the character having an 18-year-old daughter, which would have made Denbo 25 when the child was born. The actress pointed out that the real-life wife of the actor in question is likely around 50, highlighting the absurdity of the situation. Denbo's comments echo those of other actresses, such as Helen Mirren and Maggie Gyllenhaal, who have previously criticized ageist practices in the industry. Meryl Streep has also taken steps to address this issue by funding a screenwriting lab for women over 40. Denbo's public stance aims to bring attention to the pervasive ageism and sexism in Hollywood, advocating for more diverse and realistic roles for actresses of all ages.

"John Carter," directed by Andrew Stanton and based on Edgar Rice Burroughs' classic pulp stories, is a mixed bag of adventure and spectacle. The film, with its $250 million budget, aims to bring Burroughs' imaginative Martian world to life but struggles with a convoluted plot and underwhelming action sequences. Taylor Kitsch, known for his role in "Friday Night Lights," takes on the lead role of John Carter, a former Confederate soldier who finds himself on Mars. Despite Kitsch's earnest performance, the character often feels flat and the narrative is riddled with plot holes and inconsistencies.

The Martian setting, with its towering spires and barren deserts, provides a visually stunning backdrop, but the action sequences, while well-executed, lack the depth and excitement one might expect from a big-budget epic. Willem Dafoe and Lynn Collins deliver strong performances, with Dafoe's Tars Tarkas providing a welcome contrast to the more generic villainous roles. The film's reliance on Burroughs' source material is both a strength and a weakness, as it tries to balance familiar tropes with new elements, often failing to create a cohesive narrative.

Critics and audiences alike have been divided, with some praising the film's visual effects and setting while others find it overlong and underwhelming. The movie's attempt to create a new franchise is evident in its ambitious scope and its nods to Burroughs' own writing, but the execution often falls short. Ultimately, "John Carter" is a film that may appeal to fans of the source material or those looking for a fun, if flawed, adventure, but it struggles to live up to the hype and expectations surrounding its production.

U.S. Senator John McCain (R-AZ) has responded to the Syrian regime's complaint to the United Nations regarding his 2013 visit with Syrian rebels, stating that the regime's priorities are misplaced. McCain argues that the international community's inaction in addressing the Assad regime's atrocities is a "stain on our collective moral conscience." In a tweet, McCain expressed pride in achieving a "superfecta" by upsetting regimes he opposes, including Syria, Russia, Cuba, and ISIS. His other notable confrontations included Russian President Vladimir Putin's decision to put him on a sanctions list and former Cuban President Fidel Castro's accusation that McCain and Mossad were responsible for creating ISIS. The Syrian complaint, made by envoy Bashar Ja’afari, criticized McCain and other individuals for entering Syrian territory without a visa. McCain's response emphasized the regime's responsibility for the deaths of over 200,000 Syrians and highlighted the regime's focus on his visit rather than addressing the humanitarian crisis. This incident underscores the ongoing tension between McCain and the Assad regime, reflecting broader international concerns over the Syrian conflict and the effectiveness of diplomatic efforts.

Todd Kohlhepp, a South Carolina serial killer serving life in prison for seven murders, recently claimed to authorities that he has two additional victims buried near Interstate 26 in Spartanburg County. Spartanburg County Sheriff Chuck Wright is leading an investigation to verify Kohlhepp's claims. Kohlhepp, who is serving seven consecutive life sentences for multiple crimes, told investigators that the bodies are located near Interstate 26 in the Enoree area. However, a search conducted by law enforcement and cadaver dogs did not find any evidence to support his claims.

Kohlhepp's crimes span over a decade and include the murders of Scott Ponder, Beverly Guy, Brian Lucas, and Chris Sherbert in 2003, as well as the sexual assault and kidnapping of Kala Brown and the murders of her boyfriend, Charlie Carter, and the Coxie couple. Kohlhepp's claims have led to a renewed search for additional victims, with Wright emphasizing the need to follow up on these claims despite the risk of giving Kohlhepp more attention. The search involved the use of industrial X-ray machines and cadaver dogs, but no evidence was found. The investigation continues, with Wright stating that they will not stop until they have more specific information to verify.

Norway was shocked by a series of attacks carried out by Anders Behring Breivik, a 32-year-old right-wing fundamentalist Christian. Breivik, who left behind a 1,500-page manifesto, killed at least 92 people and injured 97 in Oslo and Utoya Island. The manifesto, titled "2083: A European Declaration of Independence," outlines Breivik's plan for a Christian war against multiculturalism and Muslim immigration. It also details his meticulous planning and preparation, including the purchase of chemicals and explosives. Breivik targeted the government and a youth camp, both associated with Norway's Labor Party, which he saw as a threat to European Christian civilization.

Breivik's manifesto bears similarities to Al Qaeda's declarations, with a focus on historical grievances and calls for armed resistance. He predicted a conflagration that would kill or injure more than a million people and declared that "the time for dialogue is over." Norwegian authorities have stated they are investigating whether Breivik had accomplices and whether the ammonium nitrate used in the bombing was from his farm.

The attacks raised questions about the Norwegian security services' focus on Islamic terrorism rather than right-wing extremism. The manifesto's detailed planning and the homegrown nature of the attack made it difficult for Norwegians to accept. Breivik's lawyer stated that he was motivated by a desire to bring about a revolution in Norwegian society, targeting those he saw as "cultural Marxist/multiculturalist elites."

The attacks underscored the vulnerability of even peaceful nations to domestic terrorism and the need for a broader, more inclusive approach to security.

Ashley Madison, the infidelity website, has issued a statement refuting claims that the majority of its female users are fake accounts. The company claims that the data leaked by hackers was incorrectly analyzed by Gizmodo, which had suggested that very few female members had ever checked the site for messages. Ashley Madison states that in the past week, women sent over 2.8 million messages on the platform, and 87,596 women signed up. The company also asserts that it has acquired "hundreds of thousands of new users" despite the data breach and the theft of highly personal details for over 30 million users. 

In response to reports that only a small percentage of Ashley Madison users are real women, the company maintains that the leaked data fields were misinterpreted. Ashley Madison claims that the ratio of paying men to active women is 1.2 to 1, and that women are actively engaging with the platform. However, the company does not provide details on the ratio of real to fake women, leaving the authenticity of the female users in question.

Ashley Madison's executives are in survival mode, emphasizing that the company is growing and that recent media reports predicting its imminent demise are greatly exaggerated. The company also disclosed that its founder and CEO, Noel Biderman, had left the company by mutual agreement. According to Reuters, Ashley Madison was already seeking a buyer before the breach, making it unclear whether the site can continue to operate in its current form.

The company's statement challenges the notion that the site has few genuine female users, citing the high volume of messages sent by women and the influx of new female sign-ups. However, the company provides no assurances that the messages are not generated by automated scripts. Despite the significant breach, Ashley Madison insists that it is continuing its day-to-day operations and growing, suggesting that the site may continue to operate even after the public scandal.

The Aurora, Colorado, theater shooting on July 20, 2012, left 12 dead and 58 injured, with the gunman, James Holmes, using an AR-15 assault rifle, a 12-gauge shotgun, and a Glock .40-caliber pistol. Law enforcement officials suggest Holmes had extensive target practice, evidenced by his unusually high hit rate during the attack and his proficiency with the AR-15's 100-round magazine. The suspect's apartment was found booby-trapped with explosives, and officials are searching for evidence of a gun range receipt or related information. Holmes' application for membership at a local shooting range was noted, with his answering machine message described as bizarre and unnerving.

Holmes, a 24-year-old with a neuroscience background, was a second-year graduate student at the University of Colorado. His academic credentials were questioned, with neuroscientist David Eagleman stating Holmes was merely a "mediocre" student. Holmes' résumé showed experience in dissection and basic research, but Eagleman noted it was "recipe-book stuff" that every biology student should learn. Holmes was paid a stipend of $26,000, which could have financed his arsenal of weapons and ammunition. He had difficulty with a June 7 exam and dropped out of the program three days later, leaving behind a trail of suspicious package deliveries to the campus.

The university's Graduate School Dean Barry Shur expressed shock and confusion over Holmes' motives, noting that the program admits only six students annually with top grades and test scores. The school's tight monitoring of its students did not prevent Holmes' alleged methodical planning and execution of the shooting. The case raises questions about the university's oversight and the nature of academic credentials in scientific fields.

Fort Lee, New Jersey, has initiated a crackdown on pedestrians who text while walking, issuing $85 jaywalking tickets to those caught engaging in the behavior. Chief Thomas Ripoli cites three fatal pedestrian accidents this year as a reason for the initiative, aiming to reduce distractions and increase safety. However, not everyone supports the measure, with some residents arguing that they can still look around while texting and that the fines are too high. A study by Stony Brook University found that texters are 60% more likely to veer off course than non-texters, highlighting the dangers of multitasking while walking. The study, published in Gait & Posture, also noted that texting while walking produces greater interference than talking on a cell phone, affecting gait velocity and memory recall. The research suggests that texting while walking can lead to increased cognitive distraction, reduced situation awareness, and unsafe behavior. While the initiative in Fort Lee is not a ban, it aims to raise awareness about the dangers of texting while walking.

Sixteen U.S. Postal Service workers in metro Atlanta were sentenced to federal prison for accepting bribes, ranging from $250 to $1,000, to deliver cocaine on their routes. The operation, which began in 2015, was part of a broader investigation into a drug trafficking organization. Postal workers were chosen because their positions made them less likely to be caught by law enforcement. Federal agents posed as drug traffickers to identify and recruit corrupt postal workers, recording their interactions. All defendants pleaded guilty and received sentences between three and nine years in prison, with some ordered to pay restitution or forfeiture. The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the DeKalb County District Attorney's Office, and the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General. The U.S. Attorney's Office highlighted the danger of drug trafficking and the abuse of public trust, emphasizing that postal employees are typically trusted members of the community.

The Texas State Board of Education approved a resolution, narrowly passing 7-6, requiring publishers to correct a perceived "pro-Islamic/anti-Christian bias" in future world history textbooks. The resolution cites instances of unfavorable events in Christian history being emphasized while similar events in Islamic history are glossed over. Board member Terri Leo stated the goal is to send a clear message to publishers that such bias should not occur in the future. However, critics argue the resolution is politically motivated and potentially biased. The resolution does not legally bind publishers but expresses the board's intent for more balanced textbooks. Despite opposition, the resolution aims to ensure upfront that potential biases are addressed before books reach the board for approval.

A significant dispute erupted within the Democratic Party during the 2016 presidential primary, centered around Bernie Sanders' campaign allegedly accessing and saving Hillary Clinton's voter files. The Democratic National Committee (DNC) cut off Sanders' access to his own voter files, leading to a lawsuit and accusations of sabotage. By early Saturday, the DNC agreed to restore access, but the Sanders campaign would not drop its lawsuit, citing ongoing concerns about data security and favoritism.

The controversy began when Sanders' staff, including data director Josh Uretsky, accessed Clinton's voter files through a software glitch in NGP VAN, the technology vendor. Uretsky was fired, and Sanders' campaign conducted 25 searches, saving data on Clinton's supporters, particularly those who might be swayed. This breach was seen as a significant strategic advantage, with Sanders' campaign using it to raise funds and Clinton's campaign accusing them of theft.

The DNC's decision to block Sanders' access to voter files was seen as an attempt to undermine his grassroots campaign, which was gaining momentum. The Sanders campaign accused the DNC of favoritism, while the Clinton campaign maintained that the data breach was a serious breach of trust. The dispute highlighted long-standing tensions between the party and its candidates, particularly over the perception of favoritism towards Clinton.

The situation escalated as both campaigns sought legal and public relations advantages. Sanders' campaign used the controversy to rally support and attack the DNC's neutrality. The Clinton campaign, meanwhile, accused Sanders of using the data breach as a fundraising ploy and called for an independent audit.

The dispute underscores the critical role of data in modern political campaigns and the potential for technological vulnerabilities to impact electoral outcomes. The resolution, while restoring access, did not fully resolve the underlying tensions, leaving the door open for further legal and political battles.

Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been contributing their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This document primarily discusses the GQ magazine cover story featuring 'Glee' stars Lea Michele, Dianna Agron, and Cory Monteith. The National Security Agency (NSA) continued to surveil Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other Israeli leaders, despite President Obama’s promise to limit such surveillance on U.S. allies. The initial rationale for increased surveillance was the fear that Netanyahu might launch a surprise attack on Iran. By 2013, this concern had diminished, and the focus shifted to Israel’s potential opposition to the Iran nuclear deal. Intercepts revealed that Israeli leaders were aware of the negotiations and had plans to undermine the deal by leaking its details. When Netanyahu and his aides visited Washington to lobby against the deal, the NSA monitored their conversations with Congress and Jewish-American groups.

The White House was concerned that such surveillance could be seen as a breach of congressional privacy, but it believed the information was crucial to counter Netanyahu’s campaign. To avoid leaving a trail, the NSA deleted names and personal attacks on the administration. National Security Council spokesman Ned Price stated that the U.S. only conducts foreign intelligence surveillance when there is a specific and validated national security purpose. He also emphasized the U.S. commitment to Israel’s security.

The House Select Committee on Intelligence and the office of Speaker Paul Ryan are investigating the allegations. Senator Ted Cruz criticized the administration, suggesting it views Congress as an enemy. The NSA had intercepted messages indicating Netanyahu’s intent to reveal sensitive details about the Iran talks, prompting Secretary of State John Kerry to warn the prime minister. The Journal noted that the administration used Israeli media reports as a convenient source to inform Netanyahu without revealing their prior knowledge.

This situation highlights the complex balance between national security interests and the privacy of U.S. allies, particularly in the context of sensitive international negotiations.

Innovator Matt Keiser, 38, created the world's first caffeinated beef jerky, Perky Jerky, after spilling Red Bull on a snack while skiing. The product, which contains 60 mg of caffeine per ounce, will be sold in Sports Authority stores. Keiser and his partner Brian Levin founded the company. While some New Yorkers found the taste off-putting, others appreciated the caffeine boost. Engineer Sal Bouseliman noted it provided a better post-workout energy level compared to Red Bull. The jerky, priced at $2.99 for a 1 oz. bag and $4.99 for a 2 oz. bag, combines the protein benefits of beef jerky with a caffeine hit, appealing to active lifestyles.

Lululemon Athletica Inc. faced a quality control crisis when it pulled its popular black Luon yoga pants from stores due to complaints of excessive transparency. The Taiwanese supplier, Eclat Textile Co., denied any wrongdoing, stating that all shipments had been certified and manufactured according to Lululemon's specifications. This incident, the fourth quality control issue in a year for Lululemon, has raised concerns among analysts about the company's supply chain oversight. Lululemon's shares fell by almost 5% initially but recovered to close down 2.3% on the Nasdaq. The company's aggressive quality control issues have led to a decline in its stock price, down nearly 18% in 2013. Credit Suisse analyst Christian Buss highlighted the issue, noting that Lululemon has had transparency problems with swimwear and light-colored pants in the past. Lululemon's CEO Christine Day has emphasized the company's strategy of maintaining low inventory to create scarcity and maximize prices. However, the recent scandal has prompted calls for more oversight of suppliers. Analysts at Sterne Agee suggested that Lululemon should have a stronger presence in its factories to ensure quality control. The ongoing finger-pointing between Lululemon and its supplier has left customers and investors questioning the company's management and quality control processes.

Tiger Woods, the renowned golfer, has reportedly started a serious relationship with Olympic gold medalist skier Lindsey Vonn, marking his first significant romance since his 2010 divorce from Elin Nordegren. The newly elected mayor of Juneau, Alaska, Stephen "Greg" Fisk, was found dead at his home in June 2015, leading to intense speculation about the cause of his death. Initially, police did not rule out foul play, citing the bruising and blood found at the scene. The police chief, Bryce Johnson, explained that the department had to rule out all possibilities, including the possibility of a fall, due to the lack of visible signs of foul play. Preliminary autopsy results later indicated that Fisk died of natural causes, with injuries consistent with a fall. The case garnered national attention, with the police chief acknowledging the pressure from the public's curiosity and the remote location of Juneau. Mayor Fisk, a fisheries consultant, had been sworn in just months before his death, leaving his family and the city to grieve his passing.

Lady Gaga honored David Bowie at the 2016 Grammys with a transformative performance, using Intel's technology to bring her tribute to life. Robin Williams, who passed away at the age of 63, was a beloved figure in Hollywood and among his contemporaries, known for his versatile performances and his ability to entertain audiences of all ages. His impact was particularly profound on the generation born in the 1980s and 1990s, who grew up watching his animated and family-friendly films. Williams' transition from serious roles in films like "Good Morning, Vietnam" and "Awakenings" to voice acting in "Aladdin" and "Hook" marked a significant shift in his career. His performances in these films, especially his role as the Genie in "Aladdin," were widely celebrated and integral to the film's enduring popularity among his younger audience.

Williams was known for his willingness to take on roles that were challenging and often required him to lower his profile to appeal to children. Films such as "Mrs. Doubtfire," "Jumanji," and "Flubber" showcased his ability to blend humor with heart, resonating deeply with his young audience. His performances in these films were characterized by his willingness to go to extremes, often using physical comedy and elaborate disguises to engage his audience.

As the 2000s approached, Williams returned to more serious roles, though his transition was somewhat difficult due to the changing landscape of mid-budget adult dramas. Despite this, his legacy as a star who was dedicated to entertaining his audience remained strong. His movies left indelible marks on the rec-room carpets of his young fans, who rewound and rewatched them repeatedly.

The author's personal encounters with Williams, both as a stand-up comedian and later as a rising star, provided a unique perspective on his career and personality. Williams' initial confidence in his ability to maintain his anonymity as his fame grew, as well as his later struggle with the pressures of celebrity, were particularly poignant. The "Help me" moment, a reference to Williams' desperate plea for help during a Cannes Film Festival press lunch, encapsulated the author's concern for Williams' well-being and the impact of his eventual death.

Robin Williams' multifaceted career, from his early stand-up comedy to his Oscar-winning performances, left an indelible mark on popular culture. His ability to entertain and inspire his audience, regardless of their age, made him a beloved figure and a true icon of his generation.

Oakleigh Ryan Nance, a 11-month-old infant born prematurely at 3 pounds, has been battling health issues since birth, including a severe UTI that led to stage 3 kidney reflux. Recently, she was diagnosed with a dangerous, antibiotic-resistant strain of Pseudomonas, which has caused recurring infections. Additionally, tests revealed moderate ASD and pulmonary stenosis, conditions that require surgical intervention. Oakleigh is scheduled for a 4 ½-hour procedure to address the kidney reflux, aiming to restore functionality and prevent future infections. The family is optimistic, attributing their hope to their faith, and has launched a GoFundMe campaign to cover medical expenses. Oakleigh's case highlights the challenges faced by infants with complex health issues, particularly when dealing with antibiotic-resistant bacteria. The severity of the Pseudomonas infection underscores the need for advanced medical care and the potential for complications, especially in young, immunocompromised patients.

During a South Carolina town hall, Donald Trump acknowledged that he had supported an invasion of Iraq in a 2002 interview with Howard Stern, though he stated he was not a politician at the time and was against the war by the time it started. Trump also addressed his relationship with Pope Francis, calling him a "wonderful guy" despite the pontiff's comments about his stance on immigration and building a border wall. Trump defended his use of inflammatory language, stating he can be politically correct when needed. He also discussed his fast food habits, saying he prefers McDonald's and Burger King due to cleanliness. 

In the town hall, John Kasich reflected on a viral moment where he hugged a tearful young man who found hope in his message. Kasich expressed frustration with the pace of the campaign and the importance of listening to people in need. He is coming off a strong second-place showing in New Hampshire but is not expected to perform well in the South Carolina primary. Kasich mentioned he would consider appointing New Jersey Governor Chris Christie to his Cabinet. 

Jeb Bush shrugged off South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley's endorsement of Marco Rubio, maintaining he has momentum based on poll results and town hall attendance. Bush defended his stance on marijuana, saying the term "recreational drug" is misleading due to the potency of the drug. He also shared a personal story about his wife, Columba, and how she has shaped him as a leader. 

Trump's comments on Iraq also reflect his stance in his 2000 book, where he advocated a tough policy toward "outlaw" states. Trump has repeatedly claimed he was against the Iraq War before it began, despite no evidence of him publicly stating this position. In a January 2003 interview, Trump stated, "it`s sort like either do it or don`t do it," indicating his support for a decisive action. Trump's stance on the war and his inflammatory language have been key themes in his campaign, reflecting his approach to foreign policy and his ability to connect with voters.

"Men in Black 3," released in 2012, offers a sequel that surpasses its predecessor, despite a 15-year gap since the original. The film follows veteran Agent K (Tommy Lee Jones) and his younger partner Agent J (Will Smith) as they combat the escaped alien Boris the Animal, who seeks to kill K before he can shoot off one of Boris's arms. The plot involves time travel, with Brolin playing a young K, whose uncanny resemblance to Jones was praised. The movie features a mix of action, humor, and touching moments, particularly in the final sequence at Cape Kennedy. Will Smith's performance is highlighted, but the standout is Josh Brolin's portrayal of a youthful K, which revitalizes the franchise. Despite some dated elements and confusing sequences, the film delivers an engaging and entertaining experience, with a clever time travel sequence and a touching finale.

Attorney General Eric Holder testified before the House Oversight and Government Relations Committee, denying any "cover-up" regarding the botched Operation Fast and Furious, a gun-running program that allowed illegal firearms to be smuggled to Mexican drug cartels. Holder insisted there was no attempt to hide information and accused the probe of being politically motivated. The hearing followed accusations from Republicans that top Justice officials were covering up events surrounding the program. Issa, the committee chairman, threatened to seek a contempt of Congress ruling against Holder for failing to turn over documents. Republicans released a report alleging greater knowledge and involvement of Justice Department officials in the operation than previously acknowledged. Holder stated he did not authorize the controversial tactics and that no one had been disciplined yet, despite the loss of guns used in the operation. The hearing highlighted the ongoing dispute between Republicans and Democrats over the extent of knowledge and responsibility for the operation.

President Trump launched a public feud with Nordstrom over the company's decision to discontinue carrying his daughter Ivanka's clothing line, a move that initially sparked a backlash from the White House. Maxx also dropped the line, but no further action was taken by the White House. This incident highlights the complex interplay between political influence and corporate decision-making in the modern era.

The International Professional Surrogates Association (IPSA), a non-profit organization founded in 1973, is dedicated to advancing surrogate partner therapy. IPSA supports a community of professionals, including surrogate partners, therapists, and clients, by providing ethical and qualified surrogate partners, promoting research, and offering training. Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old certified sexual surrogate, has been working in this field for 35 years, helping clients overcome sexual dysfunction and intimacy issues. His clients, ranging from 22 to 75 years old, often seek his help due to emotional baggage, PTSD, or social anxiety. Larry's sessions typically involve clients unloading their emotional issues, setting therapy goals, and gradually progressing to physical touch and trust exercises.

Larry's methods include playing naked games, physical exercises, and blindfolded trust walks. He emphasizes the importance of setting ground rules and taking "baby steps" in therapy. For instance, he helped a 35-year-old woman who had survived a car accident by addressing her fear of ridicule and helping her open up. Another client, a 70-year-old woman, overcame religious guilt and numbness through physical exercises and intimacy therapy. Larry's work is not without ethical challenges, as he must maintain emotional distance and navigate clients' romantic feelings towards him. Additionally, the legality of his work is complex, as paying for sex is illegal in the U.S., and surrogates are not always protected by law. Despite these challenges, Larry believes his work is primarily therapeutic and socially instructive, helping clients overcome deep-seated issues and gain confidence in their sexual and intimate lives.

The ousting of Tunisian President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali led to widespread jubilation, particularly regarding the fall of his wife Leila Trabelsi and her family, who were seen as symbols of corruption and excess. The Trabelsi clan, known for their mafia-like control over various sectors of the Tunisian economy, faced swift retribution from the public, with their properties and businesses being looted and burned. U.S. diplomatic cables corroborate the extent of their control and the economic harm they caused. In Tataouine, Tunisia, 30,000 Libyans have fled to this town and neighboring villages, finding shelter with Tunisian families. In Misrata, rebels accused Gaddafi's forces of using larger rockets, worsening the plight of residents. The rebels called on NATO to intervene, as the military deadlock has exposed growing international rifts over the NATO-led air strikes.

A 41-year-old homeless man, James Dirk Crudup, was apprehended by Secret Service officers after jumping the White House fence on Tuesday. He was charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court, as he had been ordered to stay away from the White House due to prior incidents. The incident was captured on CNN's "John King USA" program, showing the man lying prone on the White House lawn after being tackled by officers with guns drawn. A backpack belonging to him was being examined. The Secret Service stated that authorities did not believe he was armed. This was not an isolated incident; a 6-year-old girl had reached the White House lawn the previous Sunday by slipping between the fence pickets. The White House was secured, and the incident was resolved by 9 p.m.

On Thursday, Jurgen Klinsmann, the coach of the United States national men’s soccer team, dined with President Obama, Chancellor Angela Merkel, Nobel laureates, and astronauts in Berlin. Despite his recent losses, which jeopardized the team's qualification for the 2018 World Cup, Klinsmann remained confident in his position. However, on Monday, U.S. Soccer unexpectedly announced Klinsmann's firing. The decision came after executives Sunil Gulati and Dan Flynn met with Klinsmann at a hotel in the Los Angeles area. U.S. Soccer stated that while they believe in the quality of their players, the team's performance and growth were insufficient to continue with Klinsmann. Bruce Arena, a veteran of Major League Soccer who previously led the national team from 1998 to 2006, is expected to take over the position for the remainder of the World Cup cycle. Gulati will provide further details on the decision during a conference call with the media on Tuesday. Klinsmann's firing highlights the pressure on coaches in high-profile sports and the quick decision-making processes in sports organizations.

Mitt Romney's campaign has aggressively criticized President Obama's handling of the Middle East protests and the attacks on U.S. embassies, arguing that a Romney presidency would have led to a different outcome. During a shooting at a shopping center in Arizona, four bystanders—Bill Badger, Patricia Maisch, Roger Salzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio—played crucial roles in thwarting the gunman. The attack, which killed six, including a federal judge and a 9-year-old girl, and wounded 14, including Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, was narrowly averted when the shooter tried to reload his weapon. Maisch, a 61-year-old grandmother, wrestled away a magazine from the assailant, while Badger and Salzgeber tackled him. Zamudio, inside a nearby store, helped hold the gunman down. The shooter, 22-year-old Jared Loughner, was armed with a 9-millimeter Glock semi-automatic and had obtained it in November. Federal prosecutors charged Loughner with attempting to assassinate a member of Congress and killing a federal employee. Pima County Sheriff Clarence Dupnik criticized the state's gun laws, suggesting they might contribute to such incidents. His comments drew criticism from Arizona Senator Jon Kyl. The incident highlights the bravery of ordinary citizens and the potential for quick action to prevent larger tragedies.

James Gandolfini, best known for his role as Tony Soprano in HBO's "The Sopranos," passed away at the age of 51 after suffering a suspected heart attack during a vacation in Rome. He was set to star in the upcoming HBO series "Criminal Justice," but his untimely death left the project unfinished. Gandolfini's career spanned both television and film, including roles in "Zero Dark Thirty," "The Incredible Burt Wonderstone," and "Killing Them Softly." His work on "The Sopranos" was praised for its depth and complexity, and he was recognized for his talent and humility. Gandolfini leaves behind his wife, Deborah Lin, and two children. His death has been mourned by colleagues and fans alike, with many tributes acknowledging his impact on the entertainment industry.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un held a historic summit in Singapore, committing to work together for peace and mutual respect. The two leaders engaged in a series of diplomatic activities, including a handshake, a lunch with a prawn cocktail, and a joint signing ceremony. Trump expressed optimism about the summit, stating it had gone better than expected. U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo emphasized the importance of a comprehensive and verifiable denuclearization process, while cautioning that the summit's success was uncertain. Kim Jong Un made a rare public appearance, touring Singapore's waterfront and taking selfies with local officials.

The summit aimed to address issues of denuclearization, peace-keeping mechanisms, and mutual concerns, with North Korea rejecting unilateral nuclear disarmament. Despite the positive rhetoric, experts remain skeptical about the likelihood of North Korea completely abandoning its nuclear weapons, viewing the engagement as a means to ease sanctions. Trump has lowered expectations, focusing on establishing a relationship with Kim for a long-term negotiating process. The outcome of the summit will be crucial in determining the future of U.S.-North Korea relations and the potential for denuclearization.

France's National Assembly approved a bill allowing same-sex couples the right to marry and adopt, a move that marks the country's biggest social reform since the abolition of the death penalty in 1981. The bill, which was passed by 329 votes to 229, must now be approved by the Senate before becoming law. The legislation is part of President François Hollande's first major social reform and aligns France with 11 other countries that have legalized same-sex marriage. However, the bill faces strong opposition from the Roman Catholic Church and social conservatives, who have organized large protests against the measure. The bill's passage is seen as a significant step forward for gay rights in France, though it still faces challenges in the Senate and from opponents.

Christina Grimmie's family has expressed their gratitude for the overwhelming support they have received following her tragic death. Christina's life was not only special to her immediate family but also to everyone she touched, including fans and industry professionals. The family plans to honor Christina in the best way possible, though they are taking their time to decide on the specifics. The incident occurred when 22-year-old Christina Grimmie was shot by 27-year-old Kevin James Loibl after an autograph signing event. Loibl was quickly subdued by Grimmie's brother before taking his own life.

Actor Harrison Ford was injured after crash-landing his vintage World War II plane on a golf course in Venice, California. The emergency landing was handled skillfully, with no other casualties reported. Ford, an experienced pilot, was hospitalized and expected to undergo surgery for some injuries, but his condition was stable. His son, Ben Ford, tweeted that his father was "battered, but OK" and "an incredibly strong man." Ford's publicist stated that the injuries were not life-threatening and he was expected to make a full recovery. Dr. Sanjay Khurana, a spinal surgeon on the course, helped Ford despite the potential danger. The cause of the crash remains under investigation, but Ford reported engine trouble shortly after takeoff and tried to return to the airport. This incident highlights Ford's long history of flying, including his involvement in search and rescue operations and his past experiences with plane crashes.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued a warning letter to 23andMe, ordering the company to halt sales of its Personal Genome Service (PGS) genetic testing kit, which has been marketed without FDA approval. The FDA claims the tests have not been proven effective and could mislead consumers about their health, potentially leading to unnecessary or ineffective treatments. Since 2009, the FDA has engaged in numerous interactions with 23andMe, providing detailed feedback and requesting necessary data, but the company has failed to provide adequate information to support the safety and effectiveness of the PGS.

23andMe offers a service that detects over 240 genetic conditions and traits, including heart disease, breast cancer, and other illnesses. The company has marketed the service extensively, with about half a million users. However, the FDA's letter highlights that 23andMe has not completed the necessary validations for its intended uses, and has not provided the required information for a marketing submission.

The FDA's action reflects its concern over the potential health risks associated with direct-to-consumer genetic tests. The agency's decision could set a precedent for future regulation of such tests, ensuring that they are accurate and that consumers understand their limitations. While 23andMe has acknowledged the need to improve its compliance, the FDA's warning letter could lead to significant regulatory actions if the company fails to address the issues within the 15-day deadline.

The debate over the regulation of direct-to-consumer genetic testing is ongoing, with some arguing for greater oversight to protect consumers, while others advocate for the democratization of genetic information. The FDA's move aims to strike a balance between innovation and public safety, potentially paving the way for a more structured regulatory framework for genetic testing.

An Egyptian man, Taymour el-Sobky, was sentenced to three years in prison with hard labor for making controversial statements about married women's fidelity on a television show. According to state-run newspaper Al-Ahram, el-Sobky claimed that 30% of married women are unfaithful and ready for immorality. Video clips of his comments went viral on social media, leading to public outrage and his subsequent arrest. The court also cited his statements as potentially harming public peace and damaging public interest.

The case has drawn attention to broader issues of free speech in Egypt, particularly under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi's administration. Critics argue that the government's crackdown on dissent has expanded beyond political activists to include artists, writers, and intellectuals. For instance, author Ahmed Naji was sentenced to two years in prison for violating "public modesty" after publishing an excerpt of his novel containing a sex scene. Similarly, TV presenter Islam Behery and writer Fatma Naoot have also faced legal challenges for their work.

El-Sobky's case has parallels with the recent expulsion of Tawfiq Okasha from parliament for meeting with Israel's ambassador to Egypt. Rights lawyer Gamal Eid argues that these cases highlight how pressure and public opinion, rather than the law itself, often determine the outcome. He suggests that the government's actions are inconsistent and that the law is frequently violated or applied arbitrarily.

The broader context of these cases reflects growing concerns about the erosion of free speech and creativity in Egypt, with many activists and intellectuals fearing for their future in the country.

The Rosemont Police Department has concluded their investigation into the death of 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins, ruling her death accidental and caused by hypothermia, with alcohol and topiramate (an epilepsy medication) as contributing factors. Jenkins was found in a hotel freezer nearly 24 hours after she attended a party at the Crowne Plaza Chicago O'Hare Hotel. Surveillance footage showed Jenkins staggering through the hotel hallways, alone and visibly impaired, before entering the kitchen area. No one else was seen entering the freezer until the body was discovered.

Despite the official ruling, Jenkins' family's attorney, Larry Rogers Jr., and his colleague Sam Adam Jr., have criticized the release of graphic postmortem photographs of Jenkins' body, which were first shown to the family by police. These photos, they argue, are "graphic and disturbing images" that "raise more questions than answers." The photographs depict portions of Jenkins' body exposed, including her shirt pulled up, which could be indicative of a phenomenon known as "paradoxical undressing," where a person freezing to death removes their clothing.

The police have also released audio recordings, video surveillance footage, and other documents, including a three-dimensional digital image of the kitchen where Jenkins was found. They have identified two individuals who booked the hotel room with a fraudulent credit card, and the case is still ongoing.

While the police have stated that there is no evidence of foul play, the case has sparked numerous conspiracy theories and speculation on social media. The Cook County Medical Examiner's office had already classified Jenkins' death as accidental, with hypothermia as the cause, and alcohol and topiramate as contributing factors. The police have maintained that all leads and theories were thoroughly investigated, and the facts support the conclusion that Jenkins died accidentally.

The release of the case documents and photographs has not only raised questions but also sparked further debate and speculation about the circumstances surrounding Jenkins' death.

On September 24, 2018, a bizarre incident occurred at an airport in Mumbai, India, where a drunk passenger attempted to enter the cockpit of a Kolkata-bound IndiGo flight, claiming he needed to charge his mobile phone. The aircraft was still on the ground, and following standard operating procedures, the crew initiated the offloading of the passenger, who was then taken to the airport police station. After questioning, the individual was released without any charges being filed.
